# 1.4-1.7 Measurement and Estimating

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A **measurement** is a comparison between an unknown quantity and a standard. Everything that follows in this section is a consequence of that: because a measurement is a comparison made with a real instrument, it is never exact, and the notation we use has to carry the size of that inexactness along with the number.

## Significant digits

**Significant digits** are the valid, reliable digits in a measurement. The **last digit in a measurement is an estimated, uncertain digit** — it is the one you read off between the marks on the instrument. Every rule below follows from that idea: a digit is significant if it carries information about the measurement, and not significant if it is only there to position the decimal point.

Counting significant digits:

| Rule | Example |
|---|---|
| All non-zero digits count, and so do any zeros contained between non-zero digits | 6 s.f. in 300042 |
| **Exact numbers and constants have infinite significant digits** | a counted number, or a defined constant |
| Trailing zeros count if there is a decimal point | 3 s.f. in 200. |
| Trailing zeros do not count unless scientific notation is explicitly used | 3 s.f. in 2990, but 4 s.f. in $2.990 \times 10^{3}$ |

The last row is where marks are lost. Writing 2990 leaves the reader unable to tell whether that final zero was measured or is a placeholder, so the convention treats it as a placeholder. Scientific notation removes the ambiguity, because everything written in the mantissa is there deliberately.

## Calculating with significant digits

A result may not claim more precision than the weakest measurement that went into it. The two rules differ because addition and multiplication degrade precision in different ways.

- **Addition and subtraction:** round the result to have as many **decimal places** as the measured number with the smallest number of decimal places.
- **Multiplication and division:** round the result to have as many **significant figures** as the measured number with the smallest number of significant figures.

## Uncertainty and the two kinds of error

**Uncertainty** is the variation in measured data. It comes from two distinct sources, and telling them apart determines whether repeating the experiment will help.

| | **Systematic error** | **Random error** |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | A consistent or reproducible error that affects the **accuracy** of a measurement | An unpredictable variation in measurements |
| Caused by | Instrument, environment, or methodology | Human or environmental fluctuations |

Because systematic error is reproducible, repeating the measurement reproduces the error too; only a change of instrument or method removes it.

## Accuracy, precision, and instrument limits

- **Accuracy** is how close a measurement is to the accepted value.
- **Precision** is the repeatability of the measurement using a given instrument — which is what the number of significant figures records.
- **Instrument Limit of Error (ILE)** is the maximum amount by which a measurement made by an instrument can deviate from the true value. It is generally taken as **half of the instrument's least count**.
- **Deviation** is the amount by which a single value differs from the average.

Accuracy and precision are independent. A systematically mis-calibrated instrument can be highly precise — reading the same wrong value every time — and still be inaccurate.

## Representing an experimental result

- **Absolute uncertainty (absolute error)** is the uncertainty stated in the same units as the measurement, quoted as $x \pm \Delta x$.
- **Relative uncertainty** is the absolute uncertainty compared with the measurement itself:

$$\text{relative uncertainty} = \frac{\Delta x}{x}$$

- **Relative error** compares the result with the value it should have had:

$$\text{relative error} = \frac{\text{measured value} - \text{expected value}}{\text{expected value}}$$

- **Percentage uncertainty (percentage error)** is the relative uncertainty expressed as a percentage.

## Error propagation

When measurements are combined, their uncertainties combine too, and the rule depends on the operation.

| Operation | How the uncertainty propagates |
|---|---|
| Addition and subtraction | Add the **absolute** uncertainties |
| Multiplication and division | Add the **relative** uncertainties |
| Multiplication by an exact number | Multiply the uncertainty by that same exact number |
| Powers | For a quantity raised to the power $n$, multiply the relative uncertainty by $n$ |

Note that subtraction adds absolute uncertainties rather than cancelling them — subtracting two close measurements leaves a small result carrying the full uncertainty of both, which is why such differences are unreliable.

## Graphing data

Data is plotted to show a relationship, so the plot must be set up so the relationship, not the drawing, is what the reader sees.

- Identify the **independent** and **dependent variable** before plotting.
- **Choose simple scales.**
- **Plot the points neatly.**
- **Draw a best fit line** through the data if the points form a straight line; **draw a best fit curve** if they form a curve.
- **Check anomalous data** — either investigate it or ignore it.
- **Draw error bars** for the data, so the uncertainty in each point is visible on the graph.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Measurement** | A comparison between an unknown quantity and a standard |
| **Significant digits** | The valid, reliable digits in a measurement; the last one is estimated |
| **Uncertainty** | The variation in measured data |
| **Systematic error** | A consistent or reproducible error that affects the accuracy of a measurement; caused by instrument, environment, or methodology |
| **Random error** | An unpredictable variation in measurements, caused by human or environmental fluctuations |
| **Accuracy** | How close a measurement is to the accepted value |
| **Precision** | The repeatability of a measurement using a given instrument (its number of significant figures) |
| **Instrument Limit of Error (ILE)** | The maximum amount by which a measurement made by an instrument can deviate from the true value; generally half the least count |
| **Deviation** | The amount by which a single value differs from the average |
| **Absolute uncertainty** | The uncertainty of a measurement expressed in the units of the measurement |
| **Relative uncertainty** | The absolute uncertainty divided by the measurement |
| **Relative error** | (measured value − expected value) / expected value |
| **Percentage uncertainty** | The relative uncertainty expressed as a percentage |

# 2.5-2.7 Motion at Constant Acceleration and Falling Objects

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Uniformly accelerated motion

**Uniformly accelerated motion** is motion with constant acceleration. In the cases treated here the acceleration is constant in both magnitude and direction, and the motion is along a straight line.

Because $a$ does not change, a single set of formulas describes the whole motion — there is no need to break the journey into pieces.

## The motion formulas

Four equations relate the initial velocity $v_0$, the final velocity $v$, the acceleration $a$, the displacement $x - x_0$, and the time $t$:

$$v = v_0 + at$$

$$x = x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2} a t^{2}$$

$$v^{2} = v_0^{2} + 2a(x - x_0)$$

$$\bar{v} = \frac{v + v_0}{2}$$

Each equation omits one of the five quantities. Choosing an equation is therefore a matter of asking which quantity you neither know nor want, and picking the equation that leaves it out.

## Free fall

**Free fall** is the motion of a falling object when air resistance is negligible and the only force acting is gravity — the motion of a falling object when the action can be considered due to gravity alone.

**Galileo's hypothesis:** at a given location on Earth, and in the absence of air resistance, **all objects fall with the same constant acceleration**. The mass of the object does not enter into it.

The **acceleration due to gravity** on Earth is

$$g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^{2}$$

directed **towards the Earth's centre**.

## Working free-fall problems

Free fall is uniformly accelerated motion with $a = g$, so **the same four equations solve every scenario** — whether the object is dropped from rest, thrown downwards, or thrown upwards. An initial upward or downward velocity changes only the value of $v_0$ you substitute; it does not change which equations apply, and it does not change the acceleration, which points downwards throughout, including at the top of an upward throw.

The one habit that prevents most errors: **it is important to define the direction of gravity before doing the question**. Either fix your sign convention at the start, or state the direction explicitly in the final answer. Whether $g$ enters your equations as $+9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ or $-9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ depends entirely on which direction you chose to call positive, and mixing conventions midway through is the usual source of a sign error.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Uniformly accelerated motion** | Motion with constant acceleration |
| **Free fall** | The motion of a falling object when air resistance is negligible and the only force acting is gravity |
| **Galileo's hypothesis** | At a given location on Earth, without air resistance, all objects fall with the same constant acceleration |
| **Acceleration due to gravity ($g$)** | $9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$, directed towards the Earth's centre |

# 2.8 Graphical Analysis of Linear Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A graph of motion carries more than the quantity on its vertical axis. The **slope** and the **area** each mean something physical, and knowing which is which turns a graph into a complete description of the motion.

## The position-time graph

On a position–time graph the vertical axis gives position and the slope gives velocity.

**No motion** appears as a **horizontal straight line** — the position is not changing, so the slope is zero.

**Uniform motion** appears as a **slanted straight line**:

- The **$y$-intercept is the initial position**.
- The **average velocity is the slope of the line**.
- Because the line is straight, the **instantaneous velocity equals the average velocity** everywhere on it.
- An **intersection of two lines means the two objects meet** — at that instant they are at the same position at the same time.

**Many straight lines** joined together represent **many different velocities**, one for each segment. On each segment, **velocity = slope**.

**A curve** means the velocity is changing continuously, and the two kinds of velocity now differ:

- **Average velocity** between two points is the **slope of the straight line connecting those two points** on the curve.
- **Instantaneous velocity** at a point is the **slope of the line tangential to the curve** at that point.

## The velocity-time graph

On a velocity–time graph the vertical axis gives the velocity of an object. Here the slope gives acceleration and the area gives displacement.

**A horizontal line** means the **velocity is constant**.

**The area under the graph line is the displacement.** This gives a second way to spot two objects meeting: **they meet when the area is the same**.

**Uniformly accelerated motion** appears as a **slanted straight line**:

- The **slope is the average acceleration**.
- A **rising** line means $a > 0$; a **falling** line means $a < 0$.
- **The steeper the slope, the larger the magnitude of $a$.**

**Motion with changing acceleration** appears as a curve, and the **instantaneous acceleration is the slope of the tangent to the curve**.

## The acceleration-time graph

The third graph in the set plots acceleration against time.

## What slope and area mean

Reading these graphs is a matter of remembering two chains. Differentiating downwards, the slope of position–time gives velocity and the slope of velocity–time gives acceleration. Going the other way, the area under a velocity–time graph gives displacement. This is why the same shape means different things on different axes: a horizontal line means *no motion* on a position–time graph but *constant velocity* on a velocity–time graph, and a slanted straight line means *uniform motion* on the first and *uniform acceleration* on the second. Always check the axis label before interpreting the shape.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Average velocity (on a graph)** | The slope of the line joining two points on a position–time graph |
| **Instantaneous velocity (on a graph)** | The slope of the tangent to a position–time curve at a point |
| **Instantaneous acceleration (on a graph)** | The slope of the tangent to a velocity–time curve at a point |
| **Area under a velocity–time graph** | The displacement of the object |

# 3.1 Vectors and Scalars

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The distinction

A **vector** has both **magnitude and direction**. A **scalar** has **magnitude only, no direction**.

The distinction matters because the two kinds of quantity obey different arithmetic. Two scalars are combined by ordinary addition; two vectors are not, because their directions must be accounted for as well.

## Representing a vector

A vector is drawn as **a line and an arrow**:

- The **length** of the line represents the **magnitude**.
- The **direction** of the arrow represents the **direction** of the vector.

**Drawing to scale.** Use a ruler and a compass to draw out vectors accurately. For large vectors, make a **scale bar** and follow that scale consistently throughout the diagram — a scale is only useful if every vector in the drawing obeys it.

## Stating a direction

The single most common source of a lost mark is a magnitude given without a direction. **Either define your directions before you start solving, or include the direction in the final answer.**

For motion along one line, signs are enough:

| Direction | Sign |
|---|---|
| Up | $+$ |
| Down | $-$ |
| Right | $+$ |
| Left | $-$ |

In two dimensions, **rectangular coordinates** are used — a direction such as *40 degrees North of East*.

## The same direction, named different ways

One direction can be described in more than one correct way, depending on which axis you measure from. For instance, **30 degrees West of South is the same direction as 60 degrees South of West**: the two descriptions measure the same angle from perpendicular reference lines, so they are complementary. Similarly, an angle given as so many degrees West of North can equally be stated as an angle measured from the vertical axis.

Being able to convert between these forms is what lets you recognise that two differently worded problems are the same problem.

**If the question provides you with any compass directions, it is best to use them** in your answer — matching the question's own convention avoids conversion errors.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Vector** | A quantity with both magnitude and direction |
| **Scalar** | A quantity with magnitude only, and no direction |
| **Rectangular coordinates** | A way of stating a direction as an angle from a reference direction, e.g. 40 degrees North of East |
| **Scale bar** | A drawn reference length used so that large vectors can be represented proportionally on a diagram |

# 3.2 Addition of Vectors – Graphical Methods

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The **resultant**, or **net vector**, is the sum of two or more vectors. Vector addition is **commutative**: the order in which the vectors are added does not change the result.

## The tail-to-tip method

To find the resultant of several vectors:

1. **Move the tail of one vector to the head of another**, without changing its magnitude or its direction. Sliding a vector is allowed; rotating or rescaling it is not.
2. Repeat until all the vectors are joined head to tail.
3. **The resultant points from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector.**

Two consequences follow directly:

- **If three or more vectors form a closed polygon, there is no resultant.** The head of the last vector has arrived back at the tail of the first, so the displacement between them is zero.
- **It does not matter which order you do this in** — this is the commutative property drawn out.

A practical point for the awkward case: **if the vectors lie along one straight line, draw them on close parallel lines** so that the diagram remains readable and the head-to-tail construction is clear.

## The parallelogram method

An alternative construction for two vectors:

1. **Place the two vectors tail-to-tail.**
2. **Construct a parallelogram** with the two vectors as its sides.
3. **The diagonal drawn from the common origin is the resultant vector.**

The two methods give the same answer; the parallelogram method simply keeps both vectors starting from the same point, which is often more natural when the vectors represent forces acting at one point.

## Calculating the resultant

The **Pythagorean theorem** can be used to calculate not only the magnitude of the resultant but also its angle:

$$R = \sqrt{A^{2} + B^{2}} \qquad \theta = \arctan\!\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)$$

**These apply only if the angle between the vectors is 90 degrees.** This is the restriction that is most often forgotten. For vectors that are not perpendicular, the component method of section 3.4 is required.

## Practice

1. Draw the resultant vector and calculate the net displacement to scale for a person who walks 8 km east and then 6 km north.
2. True or false: the magnitude of a vector sum is always greater than the magnitude of either contributing vector.
3. True or false: can the magnitude of a vector ever (a) be equal to one of its components, or (b) be less than one of its components?
4. Forces of 30 N due north and 40 N due east act on a mass. What is the net, or resultant, force on the mass?

Questions 2 and 3 are answered by the constructions above rather than by calculation. Question 2 should be tested against the case where two vectors point in opposite directions; question 3 against the Pythagorean relation between a resultant and its components.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Resultant (net vector)** | The sum of two or more vectors |
| **Tail-to-tip method** | Joining vectors head to tail; the resultant runs from the tail of the first to the head of the last |
| **Parallelogram method** | Placing two vectors tail-to-tail and taking the diagonal of the resulting parallelogram from the common origin as the resultant |

# 3.3 Subtraction of Vectors, and Multiplication of a Vector by a Scalar

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Negative vectors

Two vectors are **negatives** of one another if they have the **same magnitude but opposite directions**. Writing $\vec{A} = -\vec{B}$ says exactly that: the same length, reversed.

## Subtracting vectors

There is no separate construction for subtraction. **Subtracting a vector is the same as adding its negative:**

$$\vec{A} - \vec{B} = \vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$$

So to subtract graphically, reverse the second vector and then use the tail-to-tip or parallelogram method exactly as before. Every rule for addition carries over unchanged.

## Multiplying a vector by a scalar

A vector $\vec{A}$ can be multiplied by a scalar $c$. The scalar changes the length of the vector, and its sign decides whether the direction survives:

| Sign of $c$ | Direction of the product | Magnitude of the product |
|---|---|---|
| $c$ positive | The **same** direction as $\vec{A}$ | $cA$ |
| $c$ negative | The **opposite** direction to $\vec{A}$ | $\lvert c \rvert A$ |

Multiplying by $-1$ is therefore the operation that produces the negative vector used in subtraction — the special case that ties the two halves of this section together.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Negative vectors** | Two vectors with the same magnitude but opposite directions |
| **Vector subtraction** | Adding the negative of a vector: $\vec{A} - \vec{B} = \vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$ |
| **Scalar multiplication of a vector** | Multiplying a vector by a scalar $c$; the product has magnitude $\lvert c \rvert A$ and keeps the original direction if $c$ is positive, reverses it if $c$ is negative |

# 3.4 Adding Vectors by Components

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The graphical methods of section 3.2 work only for perpendicular vectors if you want a number out of them. The component method removes that restriction, and it is the general technique.

## Vector components and resolution

Once a vector is placed in a coordinate plane, it can be broken down into an **$x$ component** and a **$y$ component**. This process is called **vector resolution**.

The components are the two perpendicular vectors that add to give the original, so the original is always the hypotenuse of the right triangle they form. Fundamental trigonometry gives them:

$$A_x = A\cos\theta \qquad A_y = A\sin\theta$$

and the reverse direction — components back to the resultant — uses the Pythagorean theorem:

$$A = \sqrt{A_x^{2} + A_y^{2}}$$

Resolving and recombining are the same relation read in opposite directions, which is why one method covers both.

## Adding vectors using components

The point of resolving is that components along the same axis are collinear, so they add as ordinary signed numbers. The steps:

1. **Resolve each vector into its $x$ and $y$ components.**
2. **Add the $x$ components of all the vectors.**
3. **Add the $y$ components of all the vectors.**
4. **Get the resultant using the Pythagorean theorem**, applied to the sum of each component:

$$R = \sqrt{\left(\sum A_x\right)^{2} + \left(\sum A_y\right)^{2}}$$

5. **Find the angle using arctan:**

$$\theta = \arctan\!\left(\frac{\sum A_y}{\sum A_x}\right)$$

Note carefully what is being squared in step 4. The Pythagorean theorem is applied once, at the end, to the two *totals* — not to each vector individually.

## Practice

A GPS receiver indicates that your home is 15.0 km away and 40.0 degrees north of west, but the only path through the woods leads directly north. If you follow the path 5.0 km before it opens into a field, how far, and in what direction, would you have to walk to reach your home?

This is a vector subtraction handled by components: resolve the displacement to home, resolve the displacement already walked, and take the difference component by component before recombining.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Vector components** | The $x$ and $y$ parts into which a vector placed in a coordinate plane can be broken down |
| **Vector resolution** | The process of breaking a vector down into its components |

# 3.5-3.6 Projectile Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The concepts

A **projectile** is an object shot through the air. Its **trajectory** is the curved flight path that it follows.

**Ignoring air resistance, the net force on an object after it is launched is gravity.** Nothing pushes it forwards once it has left the hand or the boot; the only force is downwards. That single fact generates everything else in this section.

Projectile motion is a **combination of two independent motions**:

| Component | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal motion** | **Constant velocity** — there is no horizontal force, given no air resistance |
| **Vertical motion** | **Motion with constant acceleration** — free fall under gravity |

**The horizontal and vertical motions are independent.** They share only one quantity: the clock. **The time from launch to hitting the target is the same for both motions**, and time is therefore the bridge you use to pass from one to the other.

## Projectile launched horizontally

A projectile launched horizontally has **no initial vertical velocity**.

1. **Analyse the horizontal and vertical motion separately.** Horizontally, constant $v$, giving the range $x = v_x t$. Vertically, free fall, giving the height fallen $y = \tfrac{1}{2} g t^{2}$.
2. **The velocity vector at every instant is always tangent to the parabola.**
3. **The two motions are independent**, and the flight time is shared.
4. **What affects the range?** The **horizontal velocity** and the **flight time** — and the flight time is set by the height it falls from, not by how hard it was thrown.

Point 4 is the answer to the classic question of whether a bullet fired horizontally lands at the same time as one dropped: the vertical motion knows nothing about the horizontal velocity.

**How to solve:**

- **Given the $y$ values:** calculate how much time the free fall will take, then multiply the horizontal velocity by that time to obtain the range.
- **Given the $x$ values:** find the time from $t = d/v$, then substitute that time into the vertical equations to find the height or any other quantity.

## Projectile launched at an angle

Separate the initial velocity vector into its $x$ and $y$ components:

$$v_{0x} = v_0 \cos\theta \qquad v_{0y} = v_0 \sin\theta$$

Three quantities are usually asked for:

- **Maximum height** — the height of the projectile when its **vertical velocity is zero**. The horizontal velocity is not zero there; only the vertical component vanishes.
- **Level horizontal range ($R$)** — the horizontal distance the projectile travels before returning to its original height.
- **Flight time (hang time)** — how much time the projectile is in the air.

The solving method is the same as for horizontally launched projectiles, **except that there is now an initial vertical velocity in the equations**. In other words it is the same problem as throwing an object straight up or down, run alongside a constant-velocity horizontal motion.

## Practice

A player kicks a football at an angle of 45° above the horizontal. The football has an initial velocity of 10.0 m/s. Find:

1. the flight time;
2. the maximum height;
3. the range of the football;
4. the velocity and the acceleration of the ball at the maximum height;
5. the velocity of the ball 0.5 seconds after it is launched.

Part 4 is the conceptual test in the set: use the definition of maximum height and the statement that the net force after launch is gravity.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Projectile** | An object shot through the air |
| **Trajectory** | The curved flight path followed by a moving object |
| **Maximum height** | The height of a projectile at the moment its vertical velocity is zero |
| **Level horizontal range** | The horizontal distance a projectile travels before returning to its original height |
| **Flight time (hang time)** | How much time the projectile is in the air |

# 3.8 Relative Velocity

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Relative velocity** is the velocity of one body relative to another. A velocity is never simply "the" velocity — it is always measured with respect to some frame, and when two frames are themselves moving, the velocities add as vectors:

$$\vec{v}_{AC} = \vec{v}_{AB} + \vec{v}_{BC}$$

The velocity of $A$ with respect to $C$ is the velocity of $A$ with respect to $B$ plus the velocity of $B$ with respect to $C$. Because these are vectors, they combine by the tail-to-tip or component methods, not by ordinary addition.

## Wind

Wind is the everyday case of a moving frame, and its effect depends on the direction it comes from:

| Wind | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Tailwind** | Comes from behind, **increasing** the velocity |
| **Headwind** | Comes from the front, **decreasing** the velocity |
| **Crosswind** | Comes from the side, and can influence **both** the horizontal and the vertical components |

A tailwind and a headwind are collinear with the motion, so they add and subtract as signed numbers. A crosswind is not, which is why it must be resolved into components before it can be combined.

## Worked example: crossing a river

A boat travels at 30 m/s due east across a river that is 120 m wide, and the current is 12 m/s south.

1. **What is the velocity of the boat relative to the shore?** Add the boat's velocity through the water and the current's velocity as vectors. They are perpendicular, so the magnitude follows from the Pythagorean theorem and the direction from arctan.
2. **How long does it take the boat to cross the river?** The crossing time depends only on the eastward velocity and the width of the river. The current pushes the boat south, not backwards, so it does not slow the crossing — this is the same independence of perpendicular components that governs projectile motion.
3. **How far downstream will the boat land?** Multiply the current's speed by the crossing time found in part 2.

The structure of the answer is the point: solve for the time using the component across the river, then use that time in the component along the river.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Relative velocity** | The velocity of one body relative to another |
| **Tailwind** | A wind coming from behind, increasing velocity |
| **Headwind** | A wind coming from the front, decreasing velocity |
| **Crosswind** | A wind coming from the side, which can influence both the horizontal and vertical components |

markdown:
# 4.1 Force

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The basic idea

A **force** is a push or a pull exerted by one object on another. It is a **vector**.

The phrase "by one object on another" is doing real work in that definition: a force is always an **interaction between two objects**, and both must be named.

- The **system** is the object to whom the force is exerted.
- The **agent** is the object by whom the force is exerted.

If you cannot name the agent, you have not found a force.

## What a force does

A force produces one or both of the following effects:

- **A deformation** — a change in the dimension or shape of the object.
- **A change in the state of motion** — a change in velocity.

The unit of force is the **newton (N)**, defined so that

$$1\ \text{N} = 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^{2}$$

Force is measured with a **spring scale**.

## The three factors of a force

Because a force is a vector applied at a place, three things must be specified before it is fully described:

| Factor | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Magnitude** | The strength of the force vector |
| **Direction** | The direction in which the force vector acts |
| **Point of application** | The location at which the force is exerted |

Graphically a force is represented by a vector — an arrow whose length gives the magnitude and whose direction gives the direction, drawn from the point of application.

## Types of force

There are **four fundamental forces**:

- **Gravity**
- **Electromagnetic force**
- **Strong force**
- **Weak force**

For mechanics, a more useful division is by whether contact is required.

| | **Contact forces** | **Field forces** |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | A force exerted through contact | A force exerted without contact |
| Examples | Friction ($F_{fr}$), drag force (air resistance or fluid resistance), tension ($F_T$), normal force ($F_N$), spring force ($F_{sp}$), applied force ($F_A$) | Gravity, and the other field interactions |

## The spring force and Hooke's law

**Hooke's law:** the magnitude of the force is **directly proportional to the amount of stretch or compression**, within the limit of a spring.

$$F = kx$$

- $F$ is the force exerted by the spring on the attached object, in N
- $x$ is the displacement of the spring's end from its equilibrium position, in cm
- $k$ is the **spring constant**, in N/cm

The qualifier "within the limit" is the exception to keep: **a spring becomes deformed if it is stretched beyond its limit**, and past that point the proportionality no longer holds.

## Friction

Friction is classified by the kind of relative motion involved.

| Type | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Sliding friction** | Friction arising from sliding. Divides into **static friction ($F_s$)**, caused by the tendency of no relative motion, and **kinetic friction ($F_k$)**, caused by relative motion |
| **Rolling friction** | Friction arising from rolling |
| **Fluid friction** | Friction acting when an object moves through a fluid |

**Magnitude of static friction.** Static friction is **the same as the force causing the tendency to relative motion** — it takes whatever value is needed to prevent sliding. It therefore has a **range**, with an upper limit:

$$F_s \le \mu_s F_N$$

where $\mu_s$ is the **static friction coefficient**.

**Magnitude of kinetic friction.** Once sliding has begun the friction takes a single definite value:

$$F_k = \mu_k F_N$$

where $\mu_k$ is the **kinetic friction coefficient**.

The structural difference is the thing to remember. Static friction is an inequality because it adjusts itself; kinetic friction is an equation because it does not.

**Air resistance** depends on:

- **Shape** — a streamlined shape reduces friction
- **Size** — friction increases as surface area increases
- **Speed** — friction increases with speed
- **Fluid type** — its viscosity

## Combining forces

Forces on an object combine by **vector addition**.

**Balanced forces.** Two different forces acting on the same object are balanced when they act at the **same point of application**, have the **same magnitude**, act in **opposite directions**, and act **along the same line**. A force that balances another in this way is an **equilibrant**.

**Equilibrium** is the state of an object experiencing balanced forces. Its defining condition is

$$\sum \vec{F} = 0$$

and it takes two forms: the object is **at rest**, or the object is in **uniform motion**. Both count as equilibrium, because in neither case is the velocity changing.

**Unbalanced forces** give a net force that is not zero, and an unbalanced force changes the object's motion — the object **starts moving**, **stops moving**, or **changes direction**.

## Free-body diagrams

A **free body diagram** is a physical model that represents all the forces on the system. To draw one:

- Draw **the system**;
- Draw **all the forces**, each **labelled**.

Because a free-body diagram isolates the system, it makes the vector sum in the equilibrium condition something you can actually carry out.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Force** | A push or pull exerted by one object on another; a vector |
| **System** | The object to whom a force is exerted |
| **Agent** | The object by whom a force is exerted |
| **Newton (N)** | The unit of force; $1\ \text{N} = 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^2$ |
| **Contact force** | A force exerted through contact |
| **Field force** | A force exerted without contact |
| **Hooke's law** | The magnitude of the spring force is directly proportional to the amount of stretch or compression, within the limit of a spring |
| **Spring constant ($k$)** | The constant of proportionality in Hooke's law, in N/cm |
| **Static friction** | Friction caused by the tendency of no relative motion; ranges up to $\mu_s F_N$ |
| **Kinetic friction** | Friction caused by relative motion; equal to $\mu_k F_N$ |
| **Rolling friction** | Friction arising from rolling |
| **Fluid friction** | Friction acting when an object moves through a fluid |
| **Balanced forces** | Two forces on the same object with the same magnitude, opposite directions, the same line of action and the same point of application |
| **Equilibrant** | The force that balances another force |
| **Equilibrium** | The state of an object experiencing balanced forces: at rest or in uniform motion, with net force zero |
| **Unbalanced forces** | Forces whose net sum is not zero, changing the object's motion |
| **Free body diagram** | A physical model representing all the forces on the system |

markdown:
# 4.2-4.3 Newton's First Law of Motion and Mass

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Newton's first law

Also known as the **law of inertia**:

> Every object continues in its state of rest, or of uniform velocity in a straight line, as long as no net force acts on it.

Read carefully, the law says that rest and uniform motion are the same state as far as physics is concerned. Neither requires a force to maintain it; a force is needed only to change from one to the other.

## Inertia

**Inertia** is the tendency of an object to maintain its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line.

Two points about it are examined repeatedly:

- **Inertia is not a force.** It does not appear on a free-body diagram, and it has no agent. It is a property of the object.
- **The larger the mass, the larger the inertia.**

## Inertial reference frames

Newton's first law does not hold in every frame of reference, and this is why the frame has to be specified.

- **Inertial reference frames** are reference frames in which Newton's first law does hold.
- **Non-inertial reference frames** are reference frames in which Newton's first law does not hold.

## Mass

Newton said that **mass is a quantity of matter**. Two more precise definitions are used, and they arrive at mass from completely different directions.

**Inertial mass** is defined by the response of an object to a force: mass is equal to the **ratio of the net force exerted on an object to its acceleration**.

$$m = \frac{F_{net}}{a}$$

On this definition, **mass is a measure of the inertia of an object** — the larger the mass, the smaller the acceleration a given force produces.

**Gravitational mass** is mass as used in the law of universal gravitation: it **determines the size of the gravitational force between two objects**.

## The principle of equivalence

There is no obvious reason why a quantity measuring resistance to acceleration should be the same as a quantity measuring gravitational attraction. **Newton said that inertial mass and gravitational mass are equal in magnitude** — the **principle of equivalence**.

This is what permits a single number, "the mass", to be used in both $m = F_{net}/a$ and in the gravitational force law.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Newton's first law (law of inertia)** | Every object continues in its state of rest, or of uniform velocity in a straight line, as long as no net force acts on it |
| **Inertia** | The tendency of an object to maintain its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line |
| **Inertial reference frame** | A reference frame in which Newton's first law does hold |
| **Non-inertial reference frame** | A reference frame in which Newton's first law does not hold |
| **Mass** | A quantity of matter |
| **Inertial mass** | Mass defined as the ratio of the net force exerted on an object to its acceleration; a measure of inertia |
| **Gravitational mass** | Mass as used in the law of universal gravitation; it determines the size of the gravitational force between two objects |
| **Principle of equivalence** | Inertial mass and gravitational mass are equal in magnitude |

markdown:
# 4.4 Newton's Second Law of Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The law

> The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it, and is inversely proportional to its mass. The direction of the acceleration is in the direction of the net force acting on the object.

The two proportionalities combine into

$$\sum \vec{F} = m\vec{a}$$

The statement about direction is a separate claim and is easy to overlook. Acceleration points along the **net** force, not along whichever individual force happens to be largest or most obvious.

Note also how this connects to the definition of inertial mass: rearranged as $m = F_{net}/a$, the second law *is* the definition of inertial mass, and the mass in it is a measure of how strongly an object resists being accelerated.

## Apparent weight

**Apparent weight** is the force exerted by the scale.

The distinction that matters here: **a spring scale measures weight, not mass**. What the scale reports is the force it has to exert on you, and that force is not always equal to the gravitational force on you.

## The elevator

The standard test of this is a person standing on a scale in a lift. In each case, apply the second law to the person and ask what normal force the scale must supply.

| Situation of the elevator | What the second law requires |
|---|---|
| **In equilibrium** | The acceleration is zero, so the net force on the person is zero |
| **Accelerating upward** | The net force must point upward |
| **Accelerating downward** | The net force must point downward |
| **In free fall** | The acceleration is $g$ downward, and gravity alone supplies it |

Working through the four cases with a free-body diagram is what turns the second law from a formula into a method: the reading on the scale is the unknown normal force, and it is determined by the acceleration.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Newton's second law of motion** | The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass, with the acceleration in the direction of the net force |
| **Apparent weight** | The force exerted by the scale |

markdown:
# 4.7-4.8 Solving Problems with Newton's Laws

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The starting point

**Newton's first law:** an object at rest stays at rest and an object in motion stays in motion with the same speed and in the same direction unless acted upon by an unbalanced force.

Friction enters these problems through its two magnitudes:

$$F_s \le \mu_s F_N \qquad F_k = \mu_k F_N$$

Both are proportional to the **normal force**, which is why the first step in almost every problem below is to find $F_N$.

## Translational equilibrium

**If the net force on an object is zero, then the object is in translational equilibrium.** There are two types: an object **at rest**, and an object **moving at constant velocity**.

The condition is that the net sum of forces is zero, which in two dimensions means each direction separately:

$$\sum \vec{F} = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \sum F_x = 0 \ \text{ and } \ \sum F_y = 0$$

## The inclined plane

The forces on an inclined plane are decomposed into two directions chosen to match the geometry: **perpendicular to the inclined plane**, and **parallel to the inclined plane**.

Choosing axes along and across the slope rather than horizontal and vertical is what makes the problem tractable — the motion, the normal force, and the friction all lie along those axes, so only gravity needs resolving.

For a plane at angle $\theta$:

$$F_{N} = mg\cos\theta \qquad F_{g,\parallel} = mg\sin\theta$$

and the friction that follows from that normal force is

$$F_{fr} = \mu F_N = \mu mg\cos\theta$$

When an applied force is also present, it must be resolved into the same two directions before anything else is done.

**The essential method for inclined planes:**

1. **Decompose the gravity and the applied force perpendicular to the inclined plane** to obtain the normal force.
2. **Use the normal force to yield the friction.**
3. **Resolve the equilibrium with the forces parallel to the plane** — gravity and friction.

The order is not arbitrary. Friction cannot be calculated until the normal force is known, and the normal force is set by the perpendicular direction, so the perpendicular direction must be solved first.

## Connected bodies

A **system** is any group of one or more objects we choose to consider and study. Forces on it divide into two kinds:

| | Definition |
|---|---|
| **External force** | Any force on a system from a body outside of the system |
| **Internal force** | A force between bodies of a system |

By using the idea of connected bodies, **we consider a system of objects that share the same acceleration as one object**, so that the **internal forces** — such as tension and the normal force between them — **need not be considered**. Internal forces come in pairs inside the system and cancel in the total, which is exactly why enlarging the system simplifies the problem.

Generally, **the acceleration is the net force divided by the mass of the objects**:

$$a = \frac{F_{net}}{\sum m}$$

Once the acceleration is known, the **tension force** is found by isolating a single body: the tension is the resistance force and the force on an object, such that within the whole system the tension cancels out and only the net external force remains.

**Worked cases.** Three standard configurations are treated:

- **Two boxes connected with a string and pulled at one end by a force.** The net force is the applied force; the net acceleration is that force divided by the combined mass; the tension is then found from the second law applied to the box being towed alone.
- **Two boxes connected with a rope over a pulley.** Treat both boxes as one system to get the acceleration from the net external force, then isolate one box for the tension.
- **Two connected boxes on a ramp.** The direction of motion can be obtained from the net force. The tension may be written from either box — the two expressions must agree, and checking that they do is a useful test of the working.

In every case the pattern is the same: **whole system first for the acceleration, single body second for the tension.**

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Newton's first law** | An object at rest stays at rest and an object in motion stays in motion with the same speed and direction unless acted upon by an unbalanced force |
| **Translational equilibrium** | The state of an object whose net force is zero; either at rest or moving at constant velocity |
| **System** | Any group of one or more objects we choose to consider and study |
| **External force** | Any force on a system from a body outside of the system |
| **Internal force** | A force between bodies of a system |

markdown:
# 5.1 Kinematics of Uniform Circular Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Uniform circular motion

An object that **moves in a circle at constant speed** is said to experience **uniform circular motion**.

The word *speed* is doing precise work there. The speed is constant, but the velocity is not, because the direction changes continuously — and a change of velocity is an acceleration. That is why an object in uniform circular motion is accelerating despite never speeding up.

- The **velocity vector is always tangent to the path**.
- Movement on the curve undergoes **centripetal acceleration**.
- The direction of the centripetal acceleration is **towards the centre of the curve** — perpendicular to the velocity, which is what allows it to turn the velocity without lengthening it.

## Calculating the centripetal acceleration

Take two points $A$ and $B$ on the curve, separated by an arc of length $l$. As $AB$ approaches zero, the chord and the arc become equal, and the triangle formed by the two velocity vectors becomes similar to the triangle formed by the two radii. That similarity relates the change in velocity to the arc travelled, and since acceleration is defined as the change in velocity over the change in time, the result is

$$a_c = \frac{v^{2}}{r}$$

with the direction defined as pointing **towards the centre of the curve**.

Noting that a full circuit covers a circumference $2\pi r$ in one period $T$, so that

$$v = \frac{2\pi r}{T}$$

the formula above can be rewritten in terms of the period:

$$a_c = \frac{4\pi^{2} r}{T^{2}}$$

Which version to use is decided by what the question gives you: the speed, or the time for one revolution.

## Connected curves

When two rotating objects are linked, the quantity they share depends on how they are linked:

| Connection | Quantity held in common |
|---|---|
| **Connected directly** (on the same axle or shaft) | The **angular velocity** is constant between them |
| **Connected via a belt or gears** | The **displacement** — that is, the linear distance travelled at the rim — is constant between them |

The distinction is the source of many errors. Two wheels on the same axle turn through the same angle in the same time regardless of their radii; two wheels joined by a belt pay out the same length of belt, so the one with the smaller radius must turn faster.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Uniform circular motion** | The motion of an object that moves in a circle at constant speed |
| **Centripetal acceleration** | The acceleration of an object on a curved path, directed towards the centre of the curve, of magnitude $v^2/r$ |

markdown:
# 5.3 Highway Curves, Banked and Unbanked

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Unbanked curves

**Unbanked curves** are curves that are not sloped.

When a car goes around such a curve, **friction is the centripetal force**. Nothing else is available: gravity and the normal force are both vertical, so only friction can point towards the centre of the turn.

The consequences follow immediately:

- **No friction means the car goes straight.**
- **There is NEVER a centrifugal force.** The outward sensation is not a force; it is the passenger's tendency to continue in a straight line.
- **If the friction is not sufficient, the car will tend to move more nearly in a straight line**, by Newton's first law.

**As long as the tyres do not slip, the friction is static.** If they slip, the friction becomes **kinetic**, which is bad in two ways: kinetic friction is the weaker of the two, and it acts along the direction of relative sliding rather than towards the centre. The centripetal requirement points towards the circle's centre, but kinetic friction opposes the sliding instead, **making it difficult to regain control of the car and continue around the curve**.

**Maximum velocity on an unbanked curve.** Setting the maximum static friction equal to the required centripetal force gives

$$v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu_s\, g\, r}$$

The mass appears on both sides and cancels, so **the maximum speed is independent of the mass of the car**. A loaded lorry and an empty one skid at the same speed on the same bend.

## Banked curves

**Banked turns** use a slope, hill or angle to help us turn safely.

On a banked curve the normal force is no longer vertical, so it has a horizontal component pointing towards the centre of the turn. That component can supply the centripetal force by itself.

**For every banked curve there is one speed at which no friction is required** — the **design speed** — for a bank of angle $\theta$:

$$\tan\theta = \frac{v^{2}}{rg} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad v = \sqrt{r\,g\tan\theta}$$

Away from that speed, friction makes up the difference:

- If the car travels **faster** than the design speed, friction must **increase** the centripetal force.
- If the car travels **slower** than the design speed, friction must **decrease** it.

As with the unbanked case, **the banked design speed is also independent of the mass of the car**.

## Why use banked turns?

- To allow us **not to rely on friction** when turning on a road.
- **To allow planes to turn**, since they have no road friction available at all — this is the case that shows banking is not merely a convenience.
- To allow **race cars to go at faster speeds**.
- To help with the **wear and tear on your tyres**.

## Free-body diagrams to practise

Draw and compare the free-body diagrams of:

- a car,
- a plane,
- a person on a bike.

In each, identify which force, or which component of a force, is playing the centripetal role.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Unbanked curve** | A curve that is not sloped, on which friction provides the centripetal force |
| **Banked turn** | A turn using a slope, hill or angle to help a vehicle turn safely |
| **Design speed** | The one speed, for a given banked curve, at which no friction is required |

markdown:
# 5.6 Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The statement

> Every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force that is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

**This force acts along the line joining the two particles.** The word *every* is what makes the law universal: it applies to the Earth and the Moon and equally to any two objects whatsoever.

$$F = G\,\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^{2}}$$

where $G$ is the **universal gravitational constant**:

$$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^{2}/\text{kg}^{2}$$

The inverse square in the denominator is the reason gravity weakens so quickly with separation: doubling the distance quarters the force.

## Measuring $G$

The Englishman **Henry Cavendish** measured the gravitational force between two objects in **1798**, using a device made by **John Michell**. Cavendish's own aim was to **measure the density of the Earth**, but the value of $G$ can be obtained from the same measurement — which is why the experiment is remembered under his name. The guide dates the measurement to 1978; that is an error — the year was 1798.

## Conditions for applying the formula

The law is stated for *particles*, so extended objects need care:

| Situation | Treatment |
|---|---|
| **Two particles separated by a distance $r$** | Apply the formula directly |
| **Extended objects whose size is small compared with the distance $r$** | Apply the formula directly — they behave as particles at that separation |
| **Extended objects where $r$ and the size are comparable** | The formula does not apply as it stands; **integral calculus** is required |

The middle row is the one that licenses everyday use of the law. It is only because planets are tiny compared with the distances between them that they may be treated as points.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Newton's law of universal gravitation** | Every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, acting along the line joining them |
| **Universal gravitational constant ($G$)** | $6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ |

markdown:
# 6.3 Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Principle

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Energy

**Energy**, traditionally, is the **ability to do work** — the ability of an object to produce a change in itself or in the world around it.

## Translational kinetic energy

**Translational kinetic energy** is the **energy of motion**.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Symbol** | $KE$ |
| **Unit** | J (joule) |
| **Formula** | $KE = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ |

Note that the speed is squared while the mass is not. Doubling the mass doubles the kinetic energy, but doubling the speed quadruples it — which is why stopping distances grow so sharply with speed.

## The work-energy principle

$$W_{net} = \Delta KE = KE_f - KE_i = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_f^{2} - \tfrac{1}{2}mv_i^{2}$$

**Statement: the net work done on an object is equal to the change in the object's kinetic energy.**

This gives a route from forces to speeds that never mentions time, which is what makes it useful: where the kinematic equations need the duration of the motion, the work-energy principle needs only the distance over which the force acted.

**The work-energy principle is valid only if $W$ is the net work done on the object.** This is the restriction to keep. Using the work done by a single force, when other forces are also acting, gives the wrong answer — the friction, the normal force and gravity must all be accounted for before the principle can be applied.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Energy** | The ability to do work; the ability of an object to produce a change in itself or the world around it |
| **Translational kinetic energy ($KE$)** | The energy of motion, $KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$, measured in joules |
| **Work-energy principle** | The net work done on an object is equal to the change in the object's kinetic energy |

markdown:
# 6.4 Potential Energy

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Potential energy** is the energy associated with forces that depend on the **position or configuration** of an object relative to its surroundings.

That definition distinguishes it from kinetic energy at once: kinetic energy depends on how fast something is moving, potential energy on where it is or what shape it is in.

## Gravitational potential energy

**Gravitational potential energy** is the stored energy in a system resulting from the gravitational force between the Earth and the object.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Symbol** | $PE_{grav}$, or $PE_g$ |
| **Formula** | $PE_g = mgh$, and $\Delta PE_g = mg\,\Delta h$ |

where $m$ is the mass, $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity, and $h$ is the **height above a reference level**.

The reference level is chosen, not given. Only *changes* in gravitational potential energy have physical meaning, which is why the formula is as useful in its $\Delta$ form as in its absolute one.

**Work done by an external force** to move the object from point 1 to point 2, with no acceleration, equals the change in potential energy:

$$W_{ext} = \Delta PE$$

The condition "with no acceleration" matters — if the object speeds up, some of the external work has gone into kinetic energy instead.

## Potential energy belongs to a system

**Potential energy belongs to a system, and not to a single object.** The reasoning is short and worth following:

- Potential energy is associated with a **force**;
- the force on one object is **always exerted by some other object**;
- so the energy is a property of the pair, not of either one alone.

Strictly, then, a raised book does not "have" gravitational potential energy; the Earth–book system does.

## Elastic potential energy

**Elastic potential energy** is the stored energy in an object as a result of its **change in shape** — for example in rubber bands and springs.

**Hooke's law:** the spring force is **directly proportional to the displacement of the spring and opposite in direction** to that displacement.

$$F_s = -kx \qquad PE_e = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^{2}$$

where $k$ is the **spring stiffness constant** and $x$ is the distance stretched or compressed.

The minus sign in $F_s = -kx$ is what "opposite in direction" means algebraically: stretch the spring one way and it pulls back the other. Note that the energy $\frac{1}{2}kx^2$ carries no minus sign and depends on $x^2$, so a spring stores energy whether it is stretched or compressed.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Potential energy** | The energy associated with forces that depend on the position or configuration of an object relative to the surroundings |
| **Gravitational potential energy ($PE_g$)** | The stored energy in a system resulting from the gravitational force between the Earth and the object; $PE_g = mgh$ |
| **Elastic potential energy ($PE_e$)** | The stored energy in an object as a result of its change in shape; $PE_e = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$ |
| **Hooke's law** | The spring force is directly proportional to the displacement of the spring and opposite in direction to it: $F_s = -kx$ |
| **Spring stiffness constant ($k$)** | The constant of proportionality in Hooke's law |

# 6.5-6.7 Conservative Forces and the Conservation of Mechanical Energy

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Conservative and non-conservative forces

Forces are sorted into two classes by what they do to the energy of a system.

| | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Conservative force** | **Energy is not lost**; the net work it does around a closed path is zero, $W_{net} = 0$ |
| **Non-conservative force** | **Energy is lost** — these are the forces that remove energy from the system |

The classification is not decoration: it is precisely the condition under which the conservation law below may be used.

## Mechanical energy

**Mechanical energy** is the **sum of the kinetic and potential energies in the system**:

$$E = KE + PE$$

## The principle of conservation of mechanical energy

> **When only conservative forces act on a system, its total mechanical energy is conserved.**

$$E_i = KE_i + PE_i = E_f = KE_f + PE_f$$

Written out with both forms of potential energy separated:

$$KE_i + GPE_i + EPE_i = KE_f + GPE_f + EPE_f$$

The total does not change, but the split between the terms does — that is the whole content of the principle. A ball falling converts $GPE$ into $KE$; a compressed spring released converts $EPE$ into $KE$. Solving a problem with it means writing the total at one instant, writing it at another, and setting them equal.

Everything depends on the opening clause. **Only** if the forces acting are conservative is mechanical energy conserved; where a non-conservative force such as friction is present, this equation is not the one to use.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Conservative force** | A force for which energy is not lost, with $W_{net} = 0$ |
| **Non-conservative force** | A force for which energy is lost; a force that removes energy from the system |
| **Mechanical energy** | The sum of the kinetic and potential energies in the system, $E = KE + PE$ |
| **Principle of conservation of mechanical energy** | When only conservative forces act on a system, its total mechanical energy is conserved |

# 6.8-6.9 The Law of Conservation of Energy

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Transformation of energy

**Energy can be transformed from one form to another**, and **work is done when energy is transferred from one object to another**. Transformation changes the form; transfer changes the owner. Work is the name for the second of these.

## The law

> **The total energy is neither increased nor decreased in any process.** Energy can be transformed from one form to another, and transferred from one object to another, but the **total amount remains constant**.

This is the stronger statement of which the conservation of *mechanical* energy is only a special case. Mechanical energy is conserved only when the forces are conservative; **total** energy is conserved always. Where mechanical energy appears to vanish, it has been transformed rather than destroyed.

## Energy conservation with dissipative forces

A **dissipative force** is a force that **reduces the mechanical energy but not the total energy** — friction being the standard example.

**The thermal energy produced by a constant friction force is equal to the work done by friction.** That is the accounting entry that closes the balance: the mechanical energy lost has become thermal energy, in exactly the amount that friction did work.

## Conservation of energy with gravity and friction

> **The initial mechanical energy of an object equals the final mechanical energy plus the energy transformed by friction into thermal energy.**

$$E_i = E_f \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \tfrac{1}{2}mv_i^{2} + mgh_i = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_f^{2} + mgh_f + F_{fr}d$$

The friction term appears on the **final** side of the equation, not as a subtraction from the initial side. Reading it that way keeps the physical picture straight: the energy did not disappear from the start of the motion, it arrived somewhere else by the end.

Note also that the friction term is $F_{fr}d$, a force multiplied by the **distance travelled** — so unlike the height term, it depends on the path taken and not merely on the endpoints. Sliding down a longer ramp to the same destination loses more energy to friction.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Law of conservation of energy** | The total energy is neither increased nor decreased in any process; energy can be transformed from one form to another and transferred from one object to another, but the total amount remains constant |
| **Dissipative force** | A force that reduces the mechanical energy but not the total energy, e.g. friction |

# 6.10 Power

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Power

**Power** is the **rate at which work is done**. Average power equals the work done divided by the time taken to do it, and equivalently it is the **rate at which energy is transformed**.

$$\bar{P} = \frac{W}{t} = \frac{\Delta E}{t}$$

The two expressions are the same statement because work is how energy is transferred. Power says nothing about how much work is done in total — only how quickly. A crane and a person can lift the same load through the same height, doing identical work, and differ entirely in power.

The SI unit is the **watt (W)**:

| Unit | Equivalent |
|---|---|
| 1 W | 1 J/s |
| 1 kW | 1000 W |
| 1 hp (horsepower) | 746 W |

**Force and displacement should be in the same direction** when computing the work that goes into these formulas.

## Efficiency

**Efficiency** is the ratio of the **useful power output** of the engine to the **power input**:

$$e = \frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}}$$

**Efficiency is always less than 1.0.** Two reasons are given, and they are different claims:

- **No engine can create energy** — this follows from the law of conservation of energy, so an efficiency above 1 is impossible in principle.
- **No engine can even transform energy from one form to another without some energy going to friction, thermal energy and other non-useful forms.** This is why efficiency cannot reach 1 either. The energy is not lost, but it does not appear as useful output.

The first rule rules out efficiency greater than 1; the second rules out efficiency equal to 1.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Power** | The rate at which work is done; the rate at which energy is transformed |
| **Watt (W)** | The SI unit of power; 1 W = 1 J/s |
| **Horsepower (hp)** | A unit of power equal to 746 W |
| **Efficiency** | The ratio of the useful power output of an engine to the power input |

# 7.1 Momentum and Its Relation to Force

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Momentum

**Momentum** is the **product of an object's mass and its velocity**.

$$\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$$

| | |
|---|---|
| **Vector** | Yes — its **direction is the same as its velocity** |
| **Unit** | $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ |

Momentum is a vector because velocity is a vector and mass is a positive scalar; multiplying by mass scales the velocity without turning it. This is the feature that makes momentum useful in collision problems, where the directions of the objects are the whole point.

Note the contrast with kinetic energy, which involves $v^2$ and is a scalar. Momentum depends on $v$ to the first power and keeps its direction, so two objects of equal mass moving in opposite directions at the same speed have equal kinetic energies but opposite momenta.

## Change in momentum

$$\Delta\vec{p} = \vec{p}_f - \vec{p}_i = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i = m\,\Delta\vec{v}$$

The mass factors out because it does not change during the motions considered here, so the change in momentum is simply the mass multiplied by the change in velocity.

**You must define a positive direction when solving problems involving impulse and momentum.** This is the single most common source of errors in the whole chapter. Because momentum is a vector, an object rebounding from a wall has a momentum change roughly twice its incoming momentum — a result you get only if the reversal is carried through the signs correctly.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Momentum ($\vec{p}$)** | The product of an object's mass and its velocity, $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$; a vector with the same direction as the velocity, measured in $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ |
| **Change in momentum ($\Delta\vec{p}$)** | The final momentum minus the initial momentum, equal to $m\,\Delta\vec{v}$ |

# 7.2 Conservation of Momentum

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The conservation of momentum

**Under certain circumstances momentum is a conserved quantity: when no external force is exerted on the system.** That condition is the whole of the law — it is not a general truth about momentum but a statement about isolated systems.

**Momentum of the system is conserved: the sum of the momenta of the colliding objects is the same before and after the collision.**

$$\vec{p}_{Ai} + \vec{p}_{Bi} = \vec{p}_{Af} + \vec{p}_{Bf}$$

**The law of conservation of momentum: the momentum of an isolated system of objects remains constant.**

An **isolated system** is a system in which the only significant forces are those between the objects in the system. Forces between the objects redistribute momentum inside the system; only a force from outside can change the total.

Note that this is a vector equation. In two dimensions it must be applied to each direction separately, and in one dimension the signs must be tracked — which is why a positive direction has to be fixed before you begin.

## Recoil problems

The clearest demonstrations of the law are cases where a system initially at rest breaks apart: **rocket propulsion** and **gun recoil**.

For rocket propulsion, **consider the rocket and the fuel as an isolated system with no external forces**. In the reference frame of the rocket, **the total momentum of rocket plus fuel is zero**. Since the total cannot change, it must remain zero after the fuel is expelled — and that is what drives the rocket forwards.

**After an explosion:**

- The **momenta of the two objects are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction**, so that they still sum to zero.
- The **velocities** are then

$$\vec{v}_{Af} = -\frac{m_B}{m_A}\,\vec{v}_{Bf}$$

- **The velocities depend on their relative masses**, and **the less massive object gets the greater velocity**.

The last point falls straight out of the formula: since the two momenta $mv$ must match in size, the smaller mass must carry the larger speed. This is why a rifle recoils far more slowly than the bullet leaves it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Conservation of momentum** | Momentum is conserved when no external force is exerted on the system; the sum of the momenta of colliding objects is the same before and after the collision |
| **Law of conservation of momentum** | The momentum of an isolated system of objects remains constant |
| **Isolated system** | A system in which the only significant forces are those between the objects in the system |

# 7.3 Impulse-Momentum Theorem

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Impulse

**Impulse** is the **product of the force on an object and the time interval over which it acts**.

$$\vec{I} = \vec{F}\,\Delta t$$

| | |
|---|---|
| **Vector** | Yes — its **direction is the same as the force** |
| **Unit** | $\text{N}\cdot\text{s}$ (newton-second) |

**When the force is constant**, $I = Ft$ directly. **When the force is not constant**, the impulse is the **area under a force–time graph** — which is the general definition, with the constant-force case being the special one where that area is a rectangle.

## Newton's second law in terms of momentum

$$\sum \vec{F} = \frac{\Delta\vec{p}}{\Delta t}$$

**The rate of change of momentum of an object is equal to the net force applied to it.**

This is the more general form of the second law. The familiar $\sum \vec F = m\vec a$ follows from it when the mass is constant, since then $\Delta p / \Delta t = m\,\Delta v/\Delta t = ma$.

## The impulse-momentum theorem

$$\vec{I} = \Delta\vec{p} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \vec{F}\,\Delta t = \vec{p}_f - \vec{p}_i$$

**The impulse on an object is equal to the object's final momentum minus the object's initial momentum.**

The theorem is just the momentum form of the second law with the $\Delta t$ moved across, but writing it this way makes a practical point visible: a given change in momentum can be produced by a large force acting briefly or a small force acting for longer. Since the product is fixed by the momentum change, extending the time of a collision reduces the force involved.

As with everything in this chapter, **the positive direction must be defined before you substitute anything**, since impulse and momentum are both vectors.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Impulse ($\vec{I}$)** | The product of the force on an object and the time interval over which it acts; a vector in the direction of the force, measured in $\text{N}\cdot\text{s}$ |
| **Newton's second law in momentum form** | The rate of change of momentum of an object is equal to the net force applied to it |
| **Impulse-momentum theorem** | The impulse on an object is equal to the object's final momentum minus its initial momentum |

# 8.1 Angular Quantities

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Rotational motion is described with a set of quantities that mirror the linear ones, but measure angle rather than distance. The mirror only works if angles are measured in the right unit.

## Radians

A **radian** is defined as the angle such that its **corresponding arc has the same length as the radius** of the circle it is on.

That definition is what makes the radian the natural unit for rotation: with $\theta$ in radians, the arc length and the radius are related simply by

$$l = r\theta$$

Since a full circle has circumference $2\pi r$, the conversion factor is

$$2\pi \ \text{rad} = 360^{\circ}$$

## Angular position

**Angular position** describes the angle a point is at, in reference to the incident line — the reference line from which the angle is measured.

The sign convention follows the usual mathematical one:

| Sense of rotation | Sign |
|---|---|
| **Counterclockwise** | Positive |
| **Clockwise** | Negative |

## Angular displacement

**Angular displacement** is the change in angular position:

$$\Delta\theta = \theta_2 - \theta_1$$

It is the rotational counterpart of linear displacement, and like it, it carries a sign given by the sense of rotation rather than by the total angle turned through.

## Angular velocity

**Angular velocity** is the rate of change of angular position — the rotational counterpart of linear velocity:

$$\bar{\omega} = \frac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t}$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Radian** | The angle such that its corresponding arc has the same length as the radius of the circle it is on |
| **Angular position** | The angle a point is at, in reference to the incident line |
| **Angular displacement** | The change in angular position |
| **Angular velocity** | The rate of change of angular position |
