markdown:
# 7.2 Using the Law of Universal Gravitation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

An orbit is not a special kind of motion. It is a projectile that keeps missing the ground, and once that is understood the whole of orbital mechanics follows from the two things already established: the law of universal gravitation and the centripetal force requirement.

## Newton's thought experiment

Imagine a cannonball fired horizontally from a mountain top. A cannonball is a projectile, so what happens next depends entirely on how fast it is fired.

| Launch speed | Result |
|---|---|
| Not large enough | Follows a parabolic trajectory and falls back to the ground |
| Equal to orbital velocity | Enters an orbit around Earth |
| Above orbital velocity, below escape velocity | Follows an elliptical orbit around Earth |
| Exactly escape velocity | Follows a parabolic trajectory, leaving Earth |
| Very high | Follows a hyperbolic trajectory, leaving Earth |

The pivotal case is the second. At orbital velocity, the curvature of the cannonball's path matches the curvature of Earth. The cannonball is falling exactly as it always was, but Earth's surface curves away beneath it at the same rate, so it never gets any closer to the ground.

This is what makes an orbit unremarkable: nothing has been switched off, and no new force is involved. The cannonball is still a projectile under gravity alone.

## Orbital speed

A satellite orbiting Earth at a constant height moves in uniform circular motion. The net centripetal force it needs is provided by the gravitational force, so the two expressions can be set equal:

$$\frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $M$ is the mass of Earth, and $r$ is the orbital radius — which is Earth's radius *plus* the orbital height, not the height above the surface. Forgetting to add Earth's radius is the standard error in these problems.

The satellite's own mass $m$ appears on both sides and cancels, leaving

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$$

The cancellation is the important feature. Orbital speed does not depend on the mass of the satellite at all — a bolt and a space station in the same orbit travel at the same speed. It depends only on the mass of the body being orbited and the radius of the orbit, and because $r$ is in the denominator, orbital speed decreases as altitude increases.

## Escape velocity

**Escape velocity** is the minimum velocity needed for an object to escape a celestial body's gravity without additional propulsion.

Like orbital speed, escape velocity does not depend on the mass of the escaping object. It depends on the mass and radius of the celestial body being escaped from.

This gives a striking consequence at the extreme. Black holes have such extreme gravity that their escape velocity exceeds the speed of light — which is why light cannot escape from them.

## Orbital period

The period of the orbit follows from the orbital speed and the circumference:

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$$

Since $r$ appears as $r^3$ under a square root, the orbital period is proportional to the $3/2$ power of the orbital radius. Higher orbits take longer for two compounding reasons: the circle is bigger, and the satellite is moving more slowly around it.

## Practice problem

A satellite orbits 225 km above Earth's surface. Given the mass of Earth and the radius of Earth, find the orbital speed and period of the satellite.

Begin by forming the orbital radius $r$ as Earth's radius plus 225 km, converted to metres. Then apply $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$ for the speed and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{r^3/GM}$ for the period.

## Summary

1. Orbital motion is maintained by the gravitational force acting as a centripetal force.
2. Orbital speed depends on the orbital radius; it decreases as altitude increases.
3. Escape velocity is the minimum speed required to leave a celestial body's gravitational pull. It does not depend on the escaping object's mass, but on the celestial body's mass and radius.
4. The orbital period is proportional to the $3/2$ power of the orbital radius.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Orbital velocity** | The speed at which the curvature of a projectile's path matches the curvature of Earth, so that it enters orbit; $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$ |
| **Orbital radius ($r$)** | Earth's radius plus the orbital height |
| **Escape velocity** | The minimum velocity needed for an object to escape a celestial body's gravity without additional propulsion; independent of the object's mass, dependent on the celestial body's mass and radius |
| **Orbital period** | The time for one orbit, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{r^3/GM}$; proportional to the $3/2$ power of the orbital radius |

# 7.3 Two Kinds of Mass and Einstein's Theory of Gravity

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Mass has appeared in two entirely separate roles: in $F = ma$, where it resists acceleration, and in the law of universal gravitation, where it generates attraction. There is no obvious reason why the same number should serve both purposes — and the fact that it does turns out to be the doorway to Einstein's account of gravity.

## Two types of mass

### Inertial mass

**Inertial mass** is the mass that measures an object's resistance to being accelerated. It is measured by applying a known force and observing the resulting acceleration, which gives it directly from Newton's second law:

$$m_{\text{inertial}} = \frac{F}{a}$$

If you push two objects with the same force, the heavier one — the one with the larger inertial mass — will accelerate less. Inertial mass has nothing to do with gravity in this definition; it could be measured just as well in deep space, where nothing is falling anywhere.

### Gravitational mass

**Gravitational mass** is the mass that appears in Newton's law of universal gravitation, and it determines how strongly an object participates in gravitational attraction:

$$F = G\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$$

This is a different job entirely. Here mass is not resisting anything; it is the source of a force and the thing that force acts through.

### Are these two masses the same?

Yes. According to the **principle of equivalence**, inertial mass equals gravitational mass.

This is a genuinely surprising result rather than a definition. Nothing in Newtonian physics requires that an object's stubbornness against being pushed should be numerically identical to its capacity to attract other objects. The two could have been unrelated properties, measured by unrelated experiments. That they are equal is an experimental fact, and it is the fact Einstein built his theory on.

## Einstein's theory of gravity

In Einstein's view, **gravity is not a force**. Einstein said that gravity isn't a pulling force in the way Newton thought.

Instead, mass bends space, and objects move along this curved space. An object near a massive body is not being tugged sideways off a straight path; it is travelling as straight as it can through a space that is itself curved, and the curvature is what makes the path bend.

This reframing is what makes the equality of the two masses stop being a coincidence. If gravity is a force, then an object's response to gravity depends on its gravitational mass while its resistance to that response depends on its inertial mass, and the two happening to cancel is unexplained. If gravity is instead the shape of space, then every object simply follows the same curved paths regardless of what it is made of or how massive it is — there is no separate "gravitational" property left for it to have.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Inertial mass** | The mass measuring an object's resistance to acceleration, given by $m = F/a$; with the same force applied, a larger inertial mass accelerates less |
| **Gravitational mass** | The mass appearing in Newton's law of universal gravitation, determining an object's gravitational attraction |
| **Principle of equivalence** | The principle that inertial mass equals gravitational mass |
| **Einstein's theory of gravity** | The account in which gravity is not a pulling force; mass bends space, and objects move along this curved space |

markdown:
# 8.1 Momentum and Impulse

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Newton's second law describes what a force does at an instant. Momentum and impulse describe what a force does over a stretch of time, and that turns out to be the right tool for collisions — events too brief and too violent to analyse instant by instant.

## Momentum

**Momentum** ($p$) is the product of an object's mass ($m$) and its velocity ($v$):

$$p = mv$$

| | |
|---|---|
| Units | $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ |
| Type | Vector — its direction is the same as the velocity |

Because momentum is a product of two quantities, a large momentum can come from either factor. A truck and a roller skate can have the same momentum if the skate has a much higher velocity. Mass and velocity together control collisions, and neither one on its own tells you what a collision will do.

The dependence on velocity is direct rather than squared: if velocity doubles, momentum doubles.

## Impulse

**Impulse** ($I$) is the product of a force ($F$) and the time ($\Delta t$) over which it acts:

$$I = F\,\Delta t$$

| | |
|---|---|
| Units | $\text{N}\cdot\text{s}$ |
| Type | Vector — its direction is the same as the force |

Graphically, the area under a force-versus-time graph equals the impulse. This is the same reasoning as area under a velocity-time graph giving displacement: multiplying the plotted quantity by time is exactly what an area on those axes represents. It also means impulse can be found for a force that varies during the collision, which is the realistic case — a real impact does not apply a constant force.

## The impulse-momentum theorem

The impulse delivered to an object equals its change in momentum:

$$I = \Delta p \qquad \text{that is} \qquad F\,\Delta t = m v_f - m v_i$$

The theorem is what makes impulse useful, because it links the force and duration of the collision on one side to the change in motion on the other.

The most important consequence is the trade-off between the two factors on the left. For a given change in momentum, a large $\Delta t$ implies a small $F$. Airbags work on exactly this principle: they increase the time over which the collision occurs, and since the change in momentum is fixed — the passenger must be brought to rest either way — a longer time means a smaller force.

## Applications and problem-solving tips

**Collisions.** Objects with different masses experience the same force during a collision, by Newton's third law. That force acts for the same length of time on both, so by the impulse-momentum theorem their momentum changes are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, whatever the masses; it is the *velocity* changes that depend on mass, because the same change in momentum produces a smaller change in velocity for a larger mass. The guide prints that the momentum changes depend on mass and velocity; that is an error — the momentum changes are equal and opposite, and it is the velocity changes that mass governs.

**Graphical analysis of an $F$–$t$ graph.** A positive area represents an impulse in the positive direction. Areas on opposite sides of the time axis therefore represent impulses in opposite directions, and the net impulse is the signed total.

## Key point

Momentum is conserved in isolated systems — that is, in systems with no external forces. This is the result the next section develops, and it is what allows collisions to be solved without knowing anything about the forces involved.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Momentum ($p$)** | The product of an object's mass and its velocity, $p = mv$; units $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$; a vector with the same direction as the velocity |
| **Impulse ($I$)** | The product of a force and the time over which it acts, $I = F\Delta t$; units $\text{N}\cdot\text{s}$; a vector with the same direction as the force; equal to the area under a force-time graph |
| **Impulse-momentum theorem** | The impulse delivered to an object equals its change in momentum, $\Delta p = I$ |

markdown:
# 8.2 Conservation of Momentum

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The impulse-momentum theorem applied to two colliding objects yields one of the most useful results in mechanics: under the right conditions, the total momentum of the objects does not change at all, no matter how complicated the collision between them was.

## The law of conservation of momentum

The **law of conservation of momentum** states that the momentum of any closed, isolated system does not change.

Both qualifying words are load-bearing, and each rules out a specific way the total could change:

| Term | Definition | What it excludes |
|---|---|---|
| **Closed system** | A system that does not gain or lose mass | Momentum arriving or leaving with matter |
| **Isolated system** | A system in which the net external force on a closed system is zero | Momentum changing through an outside impulse |

The isolation condition follows directly from the impulse-momentum theorem. A change in the system's total momentum requires an impulse, and an impulse requires a force acting over time — so if the net external force is zero, there is no impulse available and the total momentum cannot change.

Internal forces are not excluded, and this is the point of the law. The objects within the system may push on each other as hard as they like; by Newton's third law those forces come in equal and opposite pairs, so the impulses they deliver cancel within the system.

## Applying it to collisions

The sum of the momenta of the balls is the same before and after the collision in a closed and isolated system:

$$p_{\text{total, before}} = p_{\text{total, after}}$$

For two objects, written out in full:

$$m_1 v_{1i} + m_2 v_{2i} = m_1 v_{1f} + m_2 v_{2f}$$

Momentum is a vector, so the velocities carry signs. In a one-dimensional collision, an object moving in the negative direction contributes a negative momentum, and getting these signs right is most of the work in solving these problems.

What makes the law so powerful is what it does not require. Nothing in the equation refers to the force of the collision, its duration, or what happened during it. The before-and-after states are linked directly, and the messy interval between them can be ignored entirely.

## Recoil

**Recoil** is the standard application of the law to a system that begins at rest. Since the total momentum before is zero, and the system is closed and isolated, the total momentum after must also be zero — so the two parts move apart with momenta that are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

Because those momenta are equal while the masses are not, the lighter object must move away much faster than the heavier one to carry the same magnitude of momentum.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Law of conservation of momentum** | The momentum of any closed, isolated system does not change |
| **Closed system** | A system that does not gain or lose mass |
| **Isolated system** | A system in which the net external force on a closed system is zero |
| **Recoil** | The separation of a system initially at rest, in which the parts acquire equal and opposite momenta |

# 9.1 Work

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Work has a narrow technical meaning in physics, and the narrowness is the point: only the part of a force that acts along the direction of motion counts. Holding a heavy bag while standing still does no work at all in this sense.

## What work is

**Work** is the use of force to move an object some distance.

| | |
|---|---|
| Unit | joule (J) |
| Type | Scalar — no direction, only magnitude, which may be positive or negative |

Work is a scalar even though it is built from two vectors, force and displacement. It has no direction of its own. It does, however, carry a sign: work can be positive or negative depending on the direction of the applied force in relation to the displacement of the object. A force acting along the motion does positive work; a force opposing the motion does negative work.

## Calculating work

When the force is constant and acts in the same direction as the motion:

$$W = Fd$$

For the general case, at least part of the force must be parallel to the object's displacement, and only that parallel part contributes:

$$W = Fd\cos\theta$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between the directions of the force and the displacement.

The cosine is what performs the selection. Resolving the force into a component along the displacement and a component perpendicular to it, the parallel component is $F\cos\theta$, and it is that component that gets multiplied by the distance. The perpendicular component contributes nothing, because it does not move the object along its path at all.

Reading the formula at the extremes makes the behaviour clear:

| Angle | $\cos\theta$ | Work done |
|---|---|---|
| $\theta = 0°$ — force along the motion | $1$ | $W = Fd$, the maximum, and positive |
| $\theta = 90°$ — force perpendicular to the motion | $0$ | Zero |
| $\theta = 180°$ — force opposing the motion | $-1$ | $W = -Fd$, negative |

The middle row is the one that catches people out, and it is a direct consequence of the requirement that at least part of the force be parallel to the displacement. A force at right angles to the motion has no parallel part, so however large it is, it does no work.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Work** | The use of force to move an object some distance; a scalar with magnitude only, which may be positive or negative depending on the direction of the applied force relative to the displacement |
| **Joule (J)** | The unit of work |
| **Parallel component of a force** | The part of a force lying along the displacement, $F\cos\theta$; the only part that does work, where $\theta$ is the angle between the directions of the force and the displacement |

markdown:
# 9.2 Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Work is a transfer, and what it transfers is energy. Once that connection is made precise, a whole class of problems that would otherwise need the equations of motion can be solved in one line.

## Energy

**Energy** is the ability of an object to produce a change in itself or the world around it.

**Kinetic energy (KE)** is the energy an object has due to its motion:

$$KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$$

The velocity is squared, which is the feature that governs every kinetic energy problem. Doubling an object's speed does not double its kinetic energy — it quadruples it. This is quite unlike momentum, which is directly proportional to velocity.

## Solving kinetic energy problems

The kinetic energy formula relates three quantities, so given any two, the third follows by rearrangement.

**Finding speed from kinetic energy.** Given the mass and the kinetic energy, rearrange the formula to solve for speed:

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{2\,KE}{m}}$$

Always check the units in what you are given before substituting. A mass supplied in grams or an energy in kilojoules will produce a wrong answer that looks entirely reasonable, and this is the most common way these problems go wrong.

**Finding mass from kinetic energy.** Given the speed and the kinetic energy, rearrange for mass:

$$m = \frac{2\,KE}{v^2}$$

## The work-energy theorem

**Work** is the transfer of energy when a force moves an object.

The **work-energy theorem** states that the work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy:

$$W = \Delta KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}mv_i^2$$

This is what "transfer of energy" means quantitatively. Doing positive work on an object adds to its kinetic energy and speeds it up; doing negative work — a force opposing the motion — removes kinetic energy and slows it down. The two definitions of work, as force through a distance and as a transfer of energy, are the same statement viewed from either end.

## Finding final speed after work is done

The theorem gives a direct route to a final speed without touching the equations of motion:

1. Identify the initial speed, the applied force, and the distance moved.
2. Calculate the work done from the force and the distance.
3. Add that work to the initial kinetic energy to get the final kinetic energy, since $W = \Delta KE$.
4. Solve the kinetic energy formula for the final speed.

The advantage of this route is that it needs no time and no acceleration. Where a kinematics solution would require finding the acceleration first and then the time, the work-energy theorem connects force and distance straight to the change in speed.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Energy** | The ability of an object to produce a change in itself or the world around it |
| **Kinetic energy (KE)** | The energy an object has due to its motion, $KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ |
| **Work ($W$)** | The transfer of energy when a force moves an object |
| **Work-energy theorem** | The work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy |

markdown:
# 2.1 Reference Frames

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Mechanics** is the study of motion and force. It divides into two halves: **kinematics**, the study of motion, and **dynamics**, the study of force. Everything in this chapter is kinematics — describing how an object moves, before asking what makes it move.

## Recognising motion

An object is in motion if it changes **position** relative to a **frame of reference**. That qualification is the whole content of the idea: whether an object moves depends on your point of view.

A **reference point**, or frame of reference, is a place or background used to compare whether an object is in motion or not. It is *always assumed to be stationary*. That assumption is what makes the comparison possible at all — you cannot say something has changed position unless you have fixed on something you are treating as not changing position.

Because the frame is chosen rather than given, one object can honestly be described as moving and as at rest at the same time. The two descriptions are not statements about the object alone; each is a statement about the object *and* the background it is being compared with. Naming the frame is therefore part of the answer, not an optional extra.

## Picturing motion

A **motion diagram** is a series of images showing the positions of a moving object at equal time intervals. Its purpose is to let you visualise displacement and velocity.

The equal time intervals are what give the diagram its power. Since every gap between images represents the same amount of time, the *spacing* of the positions is a direct picture of how fast the object was going: widely spaced images mean a large change of position in that fixed time, closely spaced images mean a small one. Read across the whole diagram and you can see not only where the object went, but whether it sped up or slowed down.

The **particle model** is a simplified version of a motion diagram in which the object in motion is replaced by a series of particles. Shrinking the object to a point discards its size and shape, which are irrelevant to where it is, and leaves only the information the diagram was drawn to show.

## Vectors and scalars

Physical quantities split into two kinds.

| Kind | What it carries |
|---|---|
| **Vector** | A direction *and* a magnitude (size) |
| **Scalar** | A magnitude only, with no direction |

This distinction runs through the whole of mechanics, and the first place it bites is in the two ways of measuring how far something has gone.

## Distance and displacement

| Quantity | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Distance** | Scalar | The accumulation of path |
| **Displacement** | Vector | Distance moved in a particular **direction** |

Distance accumulates: every metre of path travelled adds to it, whichever way the object was heading at the time. Displacement, being a vector, records the direction as well, so it describes where the object ended up relative to where it started rather than how much ground it covered getting there. The two agree only when the motion never doubles back.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Mechanics** | The study of motion and force |
| **Kinematics** | The study of motion |
| **Dynamics** | The study of force |
| **Frame of reference (reference point)** | A place or background used to compare whether an object is in motion or not; always assumed to be stationary |
| **Motion** | An object is in motion if it changes position relative to a frame of reference |
| **Motion diagram** | A series of images showing the positions of a moving object at equal time intervals, used to visualise displacement and velocity |
| **Particle model** | A simplified version of a motion diagram in which the object in motion is replaced by a series of particles |
| **Vector** | A quantity which has a direction and a magnitude (size) |
| **Scalar** | A quantity which has magnitude but no direction |
| **Distance** | A scalar: the accumulation of path |
| **Displacement** | A vector: distance moved in a particular direction |

# 2.2 Average Velocity and Instantaneous Velocity

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Speed

**Speed** is the distance an object travels per unit of time:

$$v = \frac{d}{t}$$

**Instantaneous speed** is the speed at a particular moment — what a speedometer reading is.

When the speed is not constant, the single number that describes a whole journey is the **average speed**:

$$\text{average speed} = \frac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}$$

When the speed *is* constant, the motion is called **constant speed motion**, and the distinction collapses: the instantaneous speed at every moment and the average speed over the whole trip are the same number.

## Velocity

**Velocity** is speed in a given direction. Because it carries a direction it is a vector, and it can be shown with an arrow.

For motion along a straight line the direction can only be one of two ways, so there is no need to draw arrows: use $+$ or $-$ to represent direction. Do not treat this sign as decoration. Direction is very important, and the sign is where it lives in a one-dimensional calculation.

**Average velocity** is built from displacement rather than distance:

$$\text{average velocity} = \frac{\text{total displacement}}{\text{time}}$$

**Instantaneous velocity** is the velocity at a particular instant of time.

## Why speed and velocity are not interchangeable

Speed is built from distance, a scalar, and velocity from displacement, a vector. Since distance accumulates path while displacement records only the net change of position with its direction, the average speed and the average velocity of the same journey are generally different numbers, and only the second of them tells you which way the object ended up from where it started.

| | Speed | Velocity |
|---|---|---|
| Type | Scalar | Vector |
| Built from | Distance | Displacement |
| Average over a trip | Total distance ÷ total time | Total displacement ÷ time |
| At a moment | Instantaneous speed | Instantaneous velocity |
| Direction shown by | — | An arrow, or $+$ / $-$ in a straight line |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Speed** | The distance an object travels per unit of time, $v = d/t$ |
| **Instantaneous speed** | Speed at a particular moment |
| **Average speed** | Total distance divided by total time, used when speed is not constant |
| **Constant speed motion** | Motion in which the speed does not change |
| **Velocity** | Speed in a given direction |
| **Average velocity** | Total displacement divided by time |
| **Instantaneous velocity** | Velocity at a particular instant of time |

summary: Acceleration is the rate at which an object's velocity changes. Written out over an interval: a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{v_f - v_i}{t_f - t_i} where v_i is the velocity at the start of the
markdown:
# 2.4 Acceleration

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The rate at which velocity changes

**Acceleration** is the rate at which an object's velocity changes. Written out over an interval:

$$a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{v_f - v_i}{t_f - t_i}$$

where $v_i$ is the velocity at the start of the interval, at time $t_i$, and $v_f$ the velocity at the end of it, at time $t_f$.

Read the formula as a subtraction of *velocities*, not speeds. Velocity is a vector, so a change of velocity is any change in that vector, and in straight-line motion the sign of $v_f - v_i$ carries the information about which way the change points. An object whose velocity is becoming more negative has a negative acceleration in exactly the same way that one whose velocity is becoming more positive has a positive one.

## Instantaneous acceleration

**Instantaneous acceleration** is the change in velocity at an instant of time, as opposed to the average worked out across a whole interval by the formula above. The two agree whenever the acceleration is constant, and part from each other whenever it is not.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Acceleration** | The rate at which an object's velocity changes, $a = \Delta v / \Delta t = (v_f - v_i)/(t_f - t_i)$ |
| **Instantaneous acceleration** | The change in velocity at an instant of time |

title: Motion at Constant Acceleration
summary: When the acceleration does not change during the motion, the definitions of average velocity and of acceleration can be combined into a small set of equations relating the five quantities that describ
markdown:
# 2.5 Motion at Constant Acceleration

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The equations

When the acceleration does not change during the motion, the definitions of average velocity and of acceleration can be combined into a small set of equations relating the five quantities that describe the motion: initial velocity $v_i$, final velocity $v_f$, acceleration $a$, displacement $d$ and time $t$.

$$v_f = v_i + at$$

$$d = v_i t + \tfrac{1}{2} a t^2$$

$$v_f^2 = v_i^2 + 2ad$$

$$d = \frac{v_i + v_f}{2}\, t$$

The first is just the definition of acceleration, $a = (v_f - v_i)/t$, rearranged. The last is the statement that under constant acceleration the average velocity is the plain mean of the starting and finishing velocities, fed into displacement $=$ average velocity $\times$ time.

## Solving problems with them

Each equation leaves out exactly one of the five quantities, and that is what makes choosing between them mechanical rather than a matter of taste.

| Equation | Quantity it does not contain |
|---|---|
| $v_f = v_i + at$ | Displacement $d$ |
| $d = v_i t + \tfrac{1}{2} a t^2$ | Final velocity $v_f$ |
| $v_f^2 = v_i^2 + 2ad$ | Time $t$ |
| $d = \dfrac{v_i + v_f}{2} t$ | Acceleration $a$ |

The method follows from the table:

1. List what the problem gives you and what it asks for. That is three known quantities and one wanted quantity out of the five.
2. Identify the fifth — the one you neither know nor need.
3. Use the equation that omits it, and solve.

Because these are equations for *constant* acceleration only, check that assumption before reaching for them. And because velocity, acceleration and displacement are all vectors, fix a positive direction at the start of the problem and keep the signs of every quantity consistent with it throughout.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Motion at constant acceleration** | Motion in which the acceleration does not change, described by the four equations relating $v_i$, $v_f$, $a$, $d$ and $t$ |

# 2.7 Falling Objects

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Free fall

**Free fall** is the motion of a falling object when air resistance is negligible and the action can be considered due to gravity alone. Stripping out air resistance is what makes the case simple: one force, one acceleration, and the four constant-acceleration equations apply unchanged.

## From Aristotle to Galileo

Aristotle held that heavier objects fall faster. The claim survived for a very long time because it matches careless observation — but it is wrong, and the argument that displaced it was Galileo's.

**Galileo's thought experiment** and the model that came from it approach free fall sideways, through motion on an inclined plane, where the acceleration is small enough to be measured. The pattern it reveals is:

- the steeper the incline, the greater the acceleration;
- when the incline is made vertical, the acceleration reaches its maximum.

A vertical incline is nothing other than free fall, so the free-fall acceleration is the limit of a series of cases that can be measured directly. Extrapolating along that series gives the result: neglecting air resistance, all objects fall with the acceleration $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$.

**Galileo's hypothesis**: at a given location on the Earth, and in the absence of air resistance, all objects fall with the same constant acceleration.

## What the acceleration due to gravity does not depend on

The hypothesis is a strong one because of everything it declares irrelevant. The acceleration due to gravity is the same:

- no matter what the falling object is made of;
- no matter how much it weighs;
- no matter what height it was dropped from;
- no matter whether it was dropped downward or thrown upward.

The last of these is the one most often missed. An object thrown upward is in free fall the whole time it is in the air, including on the way up and at the top, because gravity is the only thing acting on it throughout.

The clause "at a given location" is doing real work too: there are small variations in $g$ at different **latitude** and **elevation** on Earth. They are small, but the constant is not universal across the planet.

## Signs and the equation for a drop from rest

Since the motion is along a line, direction is carried by a sign, and both conventions appear:

| Convention | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $+g$ | Downward is taken as positive |
| $-g$ | Upward is taken as positive |

Pick one at the start of a problem and keep every quantity consistent with it.

For an object released from rest, $v_i = 0$, and the displacement equation for constant acceleration reduces to

$$d = \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2$$

which gives the distance fallen after a time $t$. The dependence on $t^2$ rather than $t$ is why a falling object covers so much more ground in its later moments than in its first ones.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Free fall** | The motion of a falling object when air resistance is negligible and the action can be considered due to gravity alone |
| **Galileo's hypothesis** | At a given location on the Earth and in the absence of air resistance, all objects fall with the same constant acceleration |
| **Acceleration due to gravity ($g$)** | The constant free-fall acceleration, $9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$, independent of the object's material, weight, drop height and whether it was dropped or thrown upward |

# 2.8 Graphical Analysis of Linear Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Three graphs describe straight-line motion, and each one answers a different question. The skill being tested is not drawing them but reading them: knowing what a slope means on each set of axes, and what an area under the line means.

## Position–time graphs

### No motion

An object at rest gives a **horizontal straight line** — a line parallel to the $x$-axis. Position is not changing, so there is no rise.

### Uniform motion

Uniform motion gives a **slanted straight line**.

- The **$y$-intercept** is the initial position, the position at $t = 0$.
- An **intersection of two graph lines** means the two objects meet: at that instant they are at the same position at the same time.
- The **slope** gives the average velocity:

$$m = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{\text{displacement}}{\text{time interval}}$$

The steeper the line, the larger the speed, i.e. the larger $|v|$.

Because the line is straight, the velocity is constant, and then the **instantaneous velocity equals the average velocity** at every point. This is why a straight position–time line can be summarised by a single equation of motion built on the average velocity.

### Accelerated motion

Accelerated motion shows up on a position–time graph either as a set of several straight lines of different slopes, or as a curve.

- The **average velocity** between two moments is the slope of the straight line connecting the two corresponding dots on the graph.
- The **instantaneous velocity** at a moment is the slope of the *tangent* to the curve at that point.

The shape of the curve encodes both the velocity and the sign of the acceleration: the tangent's slope is the velocity, and how that slope changes from point to point tells you whether the acceleration is positive or negative.

### Distance–time graphs

A distance–time graph is not the same object as a position–time graph. Distance is a scalar that only accumulates, so a $d$–$t$ graph **does not have negative distance** and never falls back towards the axis.

## Velocity–time graphs

### Uniform motion, $a = 0$

Uniform motion gives a **horizontal line**: $v$ is constant and so $a = 0$. Reading it off,

- the height of the line at any moment is the velocity of the object at that moment;
- both the average and the instantaneous acceleration are zero, since the slope is zero.

The key result on these axes is that **the area under the $v$–$t$ graph equals the object's displacement**. Signs are respected by the area:

| Where the line lies | Displacement |
|---|---|
| Above the $t$-axis | Displacement $> 0$ |
| Below the $t$-axis | Displacement $< 0$ |

Two objects meet when the areas under their graphs are the same, since equal areas mean equal displacements.

### Uniformly accelerated motion

Uniform acceleration gives a **slanted straight line**.

- The slope is the average acceleration.
- Because the line is straight, the instantaneous acceleration equals the average acceleration: $a$ is constant.
- A **rising** line means $a > 0$; a **descending** line means $a < 0$.
- The steeper the line, the larger $|a|$.

### Motion with changing acceleration

If the acceleration itself changes, the $v$–$t$ graph curves, and the instantaneous acceleration at a particular moment is the slope of the tangent to the curve at that moment — the same tangent construction used for velocity on a curved position–time graph.

### Speed–time graphs

As with distance, speed is a scalar with no direction, so a speed–time graph has **no negative speed**.

## Acceleration–time graphs

- An object at rest, or in uniform motion, has $a = 0$ and gives a horizontal line lying along the $t$-axis.
- Uniformly accelerated motion has a constant non-zero $a$ and gives a horizontal line parallel to the $t$-axis.

## Summary of what slopes and areas mean

| Graph | Slope gives | Area under the line gives |
|---|---|---|
| Position–time | Velocity (average from a chord, instantaneous from a tangent) | — |
| Velocity–time | Acceleration (average from a chord, instantaneous from a tangent) | Displacement, signed |
| Acceleration–time | — | — |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Position–time graph** | A graph of position against time; its slope is velocity and its $y$-intercept the initial position |
| **Distance–time graph** | A graph of distance against time; distance is never negative |
| **Velocity–time graph** | A graph of velocity against time; its slope is acceleration and the area under it is displacement |
| **Speed–time graph** | A graph of speed against time; speed is never negative |
| **Acceleration–time graph** | A graph of acceleration against time; a horizontal line along the $t$-axis for $a = 0$, parallel to it for uniform acceleration |
| **Tangent** | The line touching a curve at a point, whose slope gives the instantaneous value at that moment |

# 3.1 Vectors and Scalars

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Vectors** have magnitude and direction. **Scalars** have magnitude only, no direction. Everything in this chapter follows from that one difference, because a quantity with a direction cannot be added, subtracted or multiplied by the ordinary rules of arithmetic.

## Representing vectors

### A line and an arrow

A vector is drawn as a line with an arrowhead:

- the **length** of the line represents the magnitude;
- the **direction** the arrow points represents the direction.

In print, the vector itself is written $\vec{A}$ — boldface type with a tiny arrow on top. When only the magnitude is concerned, it is written $A$ in italics, without the arrow. The notation is not decoration: $\vec{A}$ and $A$ are different quantities, and confusing them is how sign and direction errors get into an answer.

### Direction of a vector

The arrow fixes the direction, and the direction must be stated as part of any complete answer for a vector quantity.

### Drawing to scale

A vector diagram is only as good as its scale. Choose the scale so that **at least two segments are used to represent a single vector** — a vector drawn only one division long has no room to show its length accurately, and every measurement taken off the diagram inherits that error.

### Drawing in a casual way

A sketch that is not to scale is still useful for setting up a problem: it shows which vectors point which way and how they are to be combined, even when it cannot be measured. Use a casual sketch to plan, and a scale drawing when a graphical answer is wanted.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Vector** | A quantity with magnitude and direction, written $\vec{A}$ |
| **Scalar** | A quantity with magnitude only, no direction |
| **Magnitude** | The size of a vector, represented by the length of the arrow and written $A$ in italics |

# 3.2 Addition of Vectors — Graphical Methods

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The **resultant**, or net vector, is the sum of two or more vectors. Two drawings produce it, and one theorem shortcuts the drawing when the vectors happen to be perpendicular.

## The tip-to-tail method

To find the resultant of $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$:

1. Move the tail of one vector to the head of the other, **without changing the magnitude or direction** of the vector being moved. Sliding a vector about the page is allowed; turning or stretching it is not, because those are the two things that define it.
2. The resultant points from the tail of the first vector to the head of the second — or, if there are more than two, to the head of the last.

Vector addition is **commutative**:

$$\vec{A} + \vec{B} = \vec{B} + \vec{A}$$

so it makes no difference which vector you move.

### Vectors in one straight line

When the vectors lie along the same straight line the construction still applies, and it produces the familiar result that vectors in the same direction add and vectors in opposite directions subtract.

That case is worth dwelling on, because it is the counterexample to the commonest wrong instinct about vector sums: **the magnitude of a vector sum is not always greater than the magnitude of either contributing vector**. Adding two vectors can produce a resultant smaller than both.

There is, however, a ceiling: **the magnitude of the resultant of two vectors is never greater than the sum of the magnitudes of the two individual vectors**. The extreme case is the two vectors pointing the same way; every other arrangement gives less.

### More than two vectors

The same rule extends to any number of vectors: chain them head to tail in any order, and the resultant runs from the tail of the first to the head of the last.

This gives a useful test. **If three or more vectors form a closed polygon, there is no resultant** — the head of the last vector lands back on the tail of the first, so the arrow representing the sum has zero length.

## The parallelogram method

An alternative construction for two vectors:

1. Place the component vectors **tail-to-tail**.
2. Use the two vectors as adjacent sides and construct a parallelogram.
3. The **diagonal drawn from the common origin** is the resultant.

It gives the same answer as the tip-to-tail method; the choice between them is a matter of which is tidier to draw.

## The Pythagorean theorem

When the two vectors being added are at right angles, the tip-to-tail triangle is a right-angled triangle, and the resultant is its hypotenuse. Its magnitude then needs no measurement:

$$R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Resultant (net vector)** | The sum of two or more vectors |
| **Tip-to-tail method** | Moving the tail of one vector to the head of another without changing its magnitude or direction; the resultant runs from the tail of the first to the head of the last |
| **Commutative** | $\vec{A} + \vec{B} = \vec{B} + \vec{A}$: the order of addition does not affect the resultant |
| **Parallelogram method** | Placing vectors tail-to-tail, constructing a parallelogram on them, and taking the diagonal from the common origin as the resultant |

markdown:
# 3.3 Subtraction of Vectors, and Multiplication of a Vector by a Scalar

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Negative vectors

Two vectors are **negative** — that is, each is the negative of the other — if they have the **same magnitude but are 180° apart**, pointing in opposite directions. Writing $\vec{A} = -\vec{B}$ says exactly that about a pair of arrows: same length, reversed direction.

## Subtracting vectors

There is no separate rule for subtraction. Subtracting $\vec{B}$ from $\vec{A}$ *is* adding the negative of $\vec{B}$ to $\vec{A}$:

$$\vec{A} - \vec{B} = \vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$$

So the procedure is: reverse the vector being subtracted, then add it by the tip-to-tail or parallelogram method exactly as in the previous section. Every rule about resultants carries over unchanged, because the operation being carried out is an addition.

## Multiplying a vector by a scalar

A vector $\vec{A}$ can be multiplied by a scalar $c$. The result $c\vec{A}$ has magnitude $cA$, and its direction depends on the sign of $c$:

| Sign of $c$ | Magnitude of $c\vec{A}$ | Direction of $c\vec{A}$ |
|---|---|---|
| $c$ positive | $cA$ | The same as $\vec{A}$ |
| $c$ negative | $cA$ | Opposite to $\vec{A}$ |

The magnitude is $cA$ either way — a magnitude is a size and cannot be negative. All the sign of $c$ does is decide whether the arrow is stretched along its own direction or flipped and then stretched. Multiplying by $-1$ is therefore the same operation as forming the negative vector above, which is what makes subtraction a special case of scalar multiplication followed by addition.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Negative vectors** | Two vectors with the same magnitude but 180° apart, in opposite directions; $\vec{A} = -\vec{B}$ |
| **Vector subtraction** | $\vec{A} - \vec{B} = \vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$: adding the negative of the second vector |
| **Scalar multiplication of a vector** | $c\vec{A}$ has magnitude $cA$; its direction is the same as $\vec{A}$ if $c$ is positive and opposite if $c$ is negative |

# 3.4 Adding Vectors by Components

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Graphical addition is limited by the accuracy of the drawing. The component method replaces the drawing with trigonometry and gives an exact answer.

## Vector components

Once a vector is placed in a coordinate plane it can be broken down into **components** — the pair of perpendicular vectors, one along each axis, that add to give it. The process is called **vector resolution**.

The components come from the trigonometric functions of the angle $\theta$ the vector makes with the $x$-axis. Since the vector is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle whose legs are the components,

$$A_x = A\cos\theta \qquad A_y = A\sin\theta$$

Resolution is the reverse of the addition in the previous section: instead of combining two vectors into one, it splits one vector into two that are guaranteed to be at right angles, which is the arrangement that makes the arithmetic easy.

## Adding vectors using components

1. **Resolve each vector** into its $x$- and $y$-components.
2. **Add the $x$-components of all the vectors.** Their sum is the $x$-component of the resultant. Do the same for the $y$-components to get the $y$-component of the resultant.
3. **Get the resultant** from its two components.

$$R_x = \sum A_x \qquad R_y = \sum A_y$$

$$R = \sqrt{R_x^{\,2} + R_y^{\,2}} \qquad \theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{R_y}{R_x}\right)$$

Step 2 is where the method earns its keep. Components along the same axis lie along the same straight line, so they add as ordinary signed numbers — no geometry, no protractor. The only vector work left is the final step, and because $R_x$ and $R_y$ are perpendicular that step is Pythagoras plus one inverse tangent.

Keep the signs of the components: a component pointing along the negative $x$-direction enters the sum as a negative number, and dropping that sign is the standard way this calculation goes wrong.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Components** | The perpendicular vectors, one along each axis, into which a vector placed in a coordinate plane can be broken down |
| **Vector resolution** | The process of breaking a vector down into its components |

markdown:
# 3.5 Projectile Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Concepts

A **projectile** is an object shot through the air. The curved flight path it follows is its **trajectory**.

After a projectile is launched, gravity is the net force on it. Nothing else acts once it has left the hand or the barrel, which is why the analysis is so clean.

The central idea is that **projectile motion is a combination of two independent motions**:

| Component | Character of the motion |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal** | Motion with constant velocity, when there is no air resistance |
| **Vertical** | Motion with constant acceleration |

The split follows directly from the fact that gravity is the only force: gravity acts vertically, so it changes only the vertical velocity, and leaves the horizontal velocity untouched.

## Projectile launched horizontally

A projectile launched horizontally has **no initial vertical velocity**. Horizontal and vertical motion are then analysed separately:

- **Horizontal motion** — the range. Constant velocity, so $x = v_x t$.
- **Vertical motion** — the height fallen. Free fall from rest, so $y = \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2$.

The velocity vector at each instant is always **tangent to the parabola**. Its horizontal part never changes while its vertical part grows, so the vector tips further and further from the horizontal as the flight goes on. The final velocity just before the projectile hits the ground is the resultant of those two components, found by the vector addition of the previous sections.

## Independence, and the time of flight

The horizontal and vertical motions are independent, and the link that ties the two separate calculations back together is the clock: **the time from launch to hitting the target is the same for both the horizontal and the vertical motion.**

The most striking consequence, and the one worth remembering, is that **an object projected horizontally will reach the ground in the same time as an object dropped vertically** from the same height. Giving a projectile a horizontal velocity does nothing to how fast it falls, because that horizontal velocity has no vertical component for gravity to act on.

## Factors affecting the range

How far a horizontally launched projectile travels before it lands depends on two things:

- the **horizontal velocity**, since range $= v_x t$;
- the **flight time**, which is set by the height it falls.

Height enters the range only through the time it buys. A projectile launched from higher up is in the air longer, so its unchanging horizontal velocity carries it further.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Projectile** | An object shot through the air |
| **Trajectory** | The curved flight path that is followed by a moving object |
| **Horizontal motion component** | Motion with constant velocity, when there is no air resistance |
| **Vertical motion component** | Motion with constant acceleration — free fall |

markdown:
# 4.7 Solving Problems with Newton's Laws: Free-Body Diagrams

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The three-step method

Every problem in this section and the next is worked the same way, and it is worth learning the shape of the method before any particular problem.

1. **Draw a free-body diagram**, resolved into the components of the motion. Every force acting on the object appears on it, drawn along or broken into the chosen axes.
2. **Analyse the relationship between the given data and the target data** using the condition that applies — equilibrium if the object is not accelerating, Newton's second law if it is.
3. **Bring in the given data** and get the result.

Step 1 is not a formality. The equations in step 2 are read off the diagram, so a force left off the diagram is a term missing from the equation, and the answer is wrong before any arithmetic starts.

## Translational equilibrium

An object is in **translational equilibrium** if the net force on it is zero.

There are two types of translational equilibrium, and the second is the one students forget:

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| Static | The object is at rest |
| Dynamic | The object is moving at constant velocity |

Both count as equilibrium because in both the velocity is not changing, and it is a *change* of velocity that requires a net force. "In equilibrium" does not mean "not moving".

The condition $\sum \vec{F} = 0$ is a vector equation, so it holds in each direction separately:

$$\sum F_x = 0 \qquad \sum F_y = 0$$

That is what makes the free-body diagram useful: resolving the forces into components turns one vector equation into two ordinary ones.

## Worked example: an object hanging from strings

*A 20.0 N object hangs at rest from strings as shown. Find the tension force in each string.*

**Step 1.** Draw the free-body diagram of the point where the strings meet, showing the weight pulling down and the tension in each string pulling along its own direction, and resolve each tension into horizontal and vertical components.

**Step 2.** The object hangs *at rest*, so it is in translational equilibrium and both component equations apply. Horizontally, the horizontal components of the two tensions must cancel one another, since nothing else acts sideways. Vertically, the vertical components of the two tensions must together add to the weight the strings are supporting.

**Step 3.** Substitute the given weight, $20\ \text{N}$, into the two equations and solve them together for the two unknown tensions.

The structure is worth noting: two unknowns, and exactly two equations, one from each direction. That is the usual arithmetic of an equilibrium problem, and it is why resolving into components is the step that makes the problem solvable at all.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Free-body diagram** | A diagram of a single object showing every force acting on it, resolved into the components of the motion |
| **Translational equilibrium** | The condition in which the net force on an object is zero; the object is either at rest or moving at constant velocity |

title: Problems Involving Friction, Inclines
summary: Friction is a force that resists the relative motion, or the tendency of such motion, of two surfaces in contact. Because it resists motion, the direction of friction is always opposite to the motion
markdown:
# 4.8 Problems Involving Friction, Inclines

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Friction

**Friction** is a force that resists the relative motion, or the tendency of such motion, of two surfaces in contact. Because it resists motion, **the direction of friction is always opposite to the motion** — you never have to guess which way it points, you read it off the motion.

Two types have been met so far:

| Type | When it acts | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Static friction** | On objects at rest | Prevents them from starting to move; must be overcome by an applied force to initiate motion |
| **Kinetic friction** (dynamic friction) | On objects already in motion | Opposes the movement; generally weaker than static friction |

The magnitudes are set by the normal force $N$ pressing the surfaces together, through a coefficient for each case:

$$f_s \le \mu_s N \qquad f_k = \mu_k N$$

Static friction gets an inequality because it takes only the value needed to prevent motion, up to a maximum of $\mu_s N$; kinetic friction has a definite value once sliding has begun. That kinetic friction is generally weaker than static friction is why a stuck object often lurches forward once it finally breaks free: the resisting force drops the instant it starts to slide.

### Worked example: maximum acceleration of a car

*What is the maximum acceleration a car can undergo if the coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the ground is 0.80?*

**Step 1.** Draw the free-body diagram, with weight down, normal force up, and friction horizontal — friction from the road is the only forward force a car has.

**Step 2.** The car does not move vertically, so the vertical forces balance and $N = mg$. Horizontally it accelerates, so $f = ma$. The largest possible acceleration comes from the largest possible friction, which is the maximum static value $f = \mu_s N = \mu_s mg$. Then

$$ma_{\max} = \mu_s mg \quad \Rightarrow \quad a_{\max} = \mu_s g$$

The mass cancels: the answer does not depend on how heavy the car is.

**Step 3.** $a_{\max} = 0.8 \times 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2 = 7.84\ \text{m/s}^2$.

## Inclined planes

*A 5.0 kg box rests on a rough inclined plane which makes a 30° angle with the floor. Find the normal force and the friction force on the box.*

**Step 1.** Draw the free-body diagram with axes along and perpendicular to the *slope*, not horizontal and vertical, and resolve the weight into those two directions: $mg\sin\theta$ down the slope and $mg\cos\theta$ into the slope.

**Step 2.** The box *rests*, so it is in equilibrium in both directions. Perpendicular to the slope the normal force balances the perpendicular component of the weight, $N = mg\cos\theta$. Along the slope, static friction balances the component pulling the box down the slope, $f = mg\sin\theta$.

**Step 3.** Substituting $m = 5.0\ \text{kg}$, $g = 9.8\ \text{N/kg}$ and $\theta = 30°$:

$$f = mg\sin 30° = 24.5\ \text{N} \qquad N = mg\cos 30° = 42.4\ \text{N}$$

Choosing the axes along the slope is what keeps this short. With horizontal and vertical axes, both the normal force and the friction would have to be resolved and the box would be accelerating in neither direction but along neither axis either.

> The guide's worked line for this example writes the mass as 3.0 kg while quoting the results 24.5 N and 42.4 N, which are the values for the 5.0 kg box stated in the question. Use 5.0 kg.

## Connected objects

*Two boxes are connected by a cord running over a pulley, box A resting on a table with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.20 between it and the table. The mass of the cord and pulley and any friction in the pulley are ignored. Find (a) the acceleration $a$ of the system, assuming the cord does not stretch, and (b) the tension in the cord.*

The solution of connected objects divides into two approaches: **the calculation of each object separately**, and **the calculation of the whole object**. Both give the same answers here, $a = 1.4\ \text{m/s}^2$ and $T = 16.8\ \text{N}$.

**First solution — divided.** Draw a free-body diagram for each box in turn and write Newton's second law for each. Box A on the table is driven by the tension and held back by kinetic friction; the hanging box is pulled down by its weight and up by the same tension. Because the cord does not stretch, both boxes have the same acceleration, and because the cord and pulley are massless and frictionless the tension is the same throughout. That gives two equations in the two unknowns $a$ and $T$, which are solved together.

**Second solution — whole.** Treat the two boxes and the cord as a single object. The tension is now internal to that object and disappears from the equation entirely, leaving the driving weight and the retarding friction acting on the total mass, which gives $a$ in one line. The tension is then recovered by returning to one of the individual boxes.

The trade-off between the methods is the point of doing both. The whole-system method gets the acceleration fastest precisely because it hides the tension; when the tension is what you were asked for, you still have to look inside the system to find it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Friction** | A force that resists the relative motion, or the tendency of such motion, of two surfaces in contact; always directed opposite to the motion |
| **Static friction** | Friction acting on objects at rest, preventing them from starting to move; must be overcome by an applied force to initiate motion |
| **Kinetic friction (dynamic friction)** | Friction acting on objects already in motion, opposing the movement; generally weaker than static friction |

# 5.1 Kinematics of Uniform Circular Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Uniform circular motion

An object moving in a circular path at constant speed experiences **uniform circular motion**.

The **velocity vector is always tangent to the circle**. This is the reason the motion cannot be described as unaccelerated even though the speed never changes: a tangent to a circle points in a different direction at every point, so the velocity vector is being turned continuously, and since velocity is a vector, turning it *is* changing it.

## Centripetal acceleration

**Centripetal acceleration** is acceleration that points toward the centre of a circular path, causing a change in direction.

$$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}$$

where $a_c$ is the centripetal acceleration in $\text{m/s}^2$, $v$ is the speed of the object in $\text{m/s}$ and $r$ is the radius of the circular path in metres.

The motion can equally be described by how long each lap takes. Writing $T$ for the **period**, the time to complete one full revolution, the object covers one circumference in one period, so

$$v = \frac{2\pi r}{T} \qquad a_c = \frac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2}$$

and the **frequency** $f$, in hertz, is the number of revolutions per unit time — the reciprocal of the period:

$$f = \frac{1}{T}$$

Note the $v^2$ in the centripetal acceleration. Doubling the speed does not double the acceleration required to keep the object on the same circle; it quadruples it. That single fact is behind most of the results in the sections that follow.

## Check your understanding

**A satellite orbits Earth with a period of 90 minutes at a radius of 7000 km. Find its orbital speed.**

The period is $90 \times 60 = 5400\ \text{s}$ and the radius $7.0 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$, so

$$v = \frac{2\pi r}{T} = \frac{2\pi (7.0 \times 10^{6})}{5400} \approx 8.1 \times 10^{3}\ \text{m/s}$$

**Two wheels are connected by a belt, with one wheel twice the radius of the other. How do their speeds compare?**

The belt does not stretch or slip, so it moves at one speed, and that is the speed of the rim of each wheel: the two wheels have the *same linear speed at the rim*. They do not turn at the same rate, though — the larger wheel has twice as far to go round, so it completes a revolution in twice the time.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Uniform circular motion** | Motion of an object along a circular path at constant speed |
| **Centripetal acceleration** | Acceleration that points toward the centre of a circular path, causing a change in direction; $a_c = v^2/r$ |
| **Period ($T$)** | The time to complete one full revolution |
| **Frequency ($f$)** | The number of revolutions per unit time, measured in hertz (Hz); $f = 1/T$ |

title: Dynamics of Uniform Circular Motion
summary: Centripetal force is the net force directed toward the centre of a circular path that keeps an object moving in uniform circular motion. It is Newton's second law applied to the centripetal accelerati
markdown:
# 5.2 Dynamics of Uniform Circular Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Centripetal force

**Centripetal force** is the net force directed toward the centre of a circular path that keeps an object moving in uniform circular motion. It is Newton's second law applied to the centripetal acceleration of the previous section:

$$F_c = m a_c = \frac{m v^2}{r}$$

with $F_c$ in newtons.

## Identifying the source of the centripetal force

Centripetal force is not a new kind of force. It is a *role*, filled by whichever real force happens to point toward the centre in the situation at hand, and it is provided by different forces in different situations — the tension in a string for an object whirled on the end of one, static friction for a car rounding a flat curve, gravity for a satellite in orbit.

The first move in any circular-motion problem is therefore to ask which real force is supplying the centripetal force. Only then does $F_c = mv^2/r$ have anything to be set equal to.

## Effects of centripetal force on motion

What the object does depends on how the available force compares with the $mv^2/r$ that the circle demands:

| Available force | Result |
|---|---|
| Equal to $mv^2/r$ | Uniform circular motion occurs |
| Less than $mv^2/r$ | The object moves outward — the curve it follows is wider |
| Greater than $mv^2/r$ | The object moves inward — the curve it follows is tighter |

The middle row is the case that matters practically: too little force does not send the object flying off sideways, it simply means the object cannot turn as sharply as the intended circle, and it takes a wider path.

## Centripetal and centrifugal force

Centripetal force is a **real force** that keeps an object moving in a circle. That is the contrast being drawn: the inward force is the one that exists and can be identified with a rope, a road or a planet, and it is the one that belongs in your equations.

## Motion in vertical circles

A vertical circle is not uniform circular motion, because gravity helps the motion on the way down and hinders it on the way up, and the analysis at the two extreme points is different.

**At the top of a loop**, gravity points toward the centre of the circle, so gravity itself can supply some or all of the centripetal force. The limiting case is when it supplies *all* of it and the string or track contributes nothing. That defines the minimum speed for staying on a circular path:

$$mg = \frac{mv^2}{r} \quad \Rightarrow \quad v_{\min} = \sqrt{gr}$$

Below that speed the required centripetal force would be less than the object's own weight, and there is no way to reduce gravity, so the object leaves the circular path.

**At the bottom of a loop**, tension is greatest. There gravity points *away* from the centre, so the tension has to supply the whole centripetal force and hold up the weight as well.

## Check your understanding

**A car makes a turn on an icy road and starts sliding outward. Explain why this happens in terms of centripetal force.**

The centripetal force for a turn on a flat road comes from friction between the tyres and the road. Ice greatly reduces the friction available, so the inward force falls short of the $mv^2/r$ the turn requires. As the table above says, a force less than the required one means the car cannot follow the intended circle and instead takes a wider path — which is what "sliding outward" is.

**A 5.0 kg object is swung in a 1.5 m radius vertical circle. Find the minimum speed needed at the top to maintain circular motion.**

$$v_{\min} = \sqrt{gr} = \sqrt{9.8 \times 1.5} \approx 3.8\ \text{m/s}$$

The mass cancels out of $mg = mv^2/r$, so the 5.0 kg is not needed.

**A satellite is in orbit around Earth. If its speed doubles while maintaining the same radius, by what factor does the required centripetal force change?**

$F_c = mv^2/r$ depends on the square of the speed, so doubling $v$ multiplies the required force by four.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Centripetal force** | The net force directed toward the centre of a circular path that keeps an object moving in uniform circular motion; $F_c = mv^2/r$ |
| **Minimum speed at the top of a vertical circle** | $v_{\min} = \sqrt{gr}$, the speed at which gravity alone supplies the centripetal force |

title: Highway Curves, Banked and Unbanked
summary: On a flat curve the centripetal force — the force that keeps a car moving in a circle — is provided by static friction if there is no other force. Nothing else on a flat road points toward the centre
markdown:
# 5.3 Highway Curves, Banked and Unbanked

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Unbanked curves

On a flat curve the centripetal force — the force that keeps a car moving in a circle — **is provided by static friction if there is no other force**. Nothing else on a flat road points toward the centre of the turn, so friction has the job on its own.

$$f_s = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$

For a car of mass $1000\ \text{kg}$ moving at $14\ \text{m/s}$ on a flat curve of radius $50\ \text{m}$, the centripetal force needed is

$$F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{1000 \times 14^2}{50} = 3.9 \times 10^{3}\ \text{N}$$

and friction must be able to supply that much, or the car does not make the turn.

Since the friction available is at most $\mu_s N = \mu_s mg$, setting that against the requirement gives the maximum speed:

$$\frac{mv_{\max}^2}{r} = \mu_s m g \quad \Rightarrow \quad v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g r}$$

The mass cancels, so **the maximum speed on an unbanked curve is determined by the friction coefficient** and the radius, not by how heavy the vehicle is.

## Banked curves

**Banked curves** are curves that are tilted to help vehicles turn without relying on friction. Tilting the road tilts the normal force with it, and the normal force then has a horizontal component pointing toward the centre of the turn — a source of centripetal force that does not depend on the state of the tyres or the road surface.

For a given bank angle $\theta$ there is one speed at which that component is exactly the centripetal force required, and no friction is needed at all:

$$\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg} \quad \Rightarrow \quad v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$$

For a curve of radius $100\ \text{m}$ banked at $15.0°$, the ideal speed is

$$v = \sqrt{100 \times 9.8 \times \tan 15.0°} \approx 16.2\ \text{m/s}$$

## When the speed is not the ideal speed

The ideal speed is a single value, and real traffic does not travel at exactly one speed, so friction returns as a correction rather than as the main effect:

| Speed | What friction does |
|---|---|
| Too fast | Friction increases to help keep the car from sliding **outward** |
| Too slow | Friction is needed to keep the car from sliding toward the **inside** of the curve |

The second case is the one that surprises people. Below the ideal speed the horizontal component of the normal force is *more* than the turn requires, so the surplus pushes the car down the bank toward the inside, and friction has to act up the slope to hold it on course.

## Check your understanding

**What happens if a car takes a turn on an unbanked curve with insufficient friction?**

Friction is the only source of centripetal force on a flat curve, so if it cannot supply the $mv^2/r$ the turn requires, the net inward force is too small and the car cannot turn as sharply as the curve demands. It slides outward, following a wider path than the road.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Unbanked (flat) curve** | A curve on which the centripetal force is provided by static friction alone |
| **Banked curve** | A curve that is tilted to help vehicles turn without relying on friction |
| **Ideal (design) speed** | The speed $v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$ at which a banked curve can be taken with no friction needed |

markdown:
# 5.6 Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The law

Every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. This force acts along the line joining the two particles.

$$F = G\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $F$ | The gravitational force |
| $G$ | The universal gravitational constant, $6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ |
| $m_1,\ m_2$ | The masses of the two objects |
| $r$ | The distance between the **centres** of the two objects |

The word *universal* is the claim being made: the same law and the same constant govern the attraction between any two masses anywhere, which is why one formula covers a falling apple, the Moon's orbit and the Earth's orbit alike.

Two features of the algebra are worth reading off directly. The force depends on the **product** of the masses, so if the mass of one planet doubles, the gravitational force doubles. The distance appears as an **inverse square**, so the force falls away far faster with separation than it grows with mass: doubling $r$ cuts the force to a quarter.

Note also that $r$ is measured between the centres of the objects, not between their surfaces.

## The Cavendish experiment

The law can be written down without knowing $G$, but nothing can be calculated from it until $G$ has a number. In 1798 **Henry Cavendish** used a **torsion balance** to measure the gravitational force between two objects in the laboratory, which allowed the universal gravitational constant $G$ to be calculated.

The measurement is difficult because gravitational attraction between laboratory-sized masses is extremely weak — which is the physical meaning of $G$ being so small a number.

## Important constants

| Constant | Value |
|---|---|
| Universal gravitational constant, $G$ | $6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ |
| Mass of Earth | $5.972 \times 10^{24}\ \text{kg}$ |
| Radius of Earth | $6.38 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$ |

The guide tabulates several further constants for problems on this scale: the mass of the Moon and the Earth–Moon distance, the mass of the Sun and the Earth–Sun distance (one **astronomical unit**, 1 AU), the speed of light, and the **light year**, the distance light travels in a year.

## Worked example

*Find the gravitational force between the Sun and the Earth.*

Substitute the mass of the Sun for $m_1$, the mass of the Earth for $m_2$, and the Earth–Sun distance of 1 AU for $r$ into $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$. The answer is in newtons.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Newton's law of universal gravitation** | Every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, acting along the line joining them |
| **Universal gravitational constant ($G$)** | The constant of proportionality in the law of universal gravitation, $6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ |
| **Cavendish experiment** | Henry Cavendish's 1798 measurement, using a torsion balance, of the gravitational force between two objects, which allowed $G$ to be calculated |
| **Astronomical unit (AU)** | The distance between the Earth and the Sun |
| **Light year** | The distance light travels in one year |
