markdown:
# 5.7 Gravity Near the Earth's Surface: Geophysical Applications

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Where $g$ comes from

The acceleration due to gravity is not an independent fact about the world. It follows from the law of universal gravitation applied to one particular pair of objects: an object of mass $m$ and the Earth.

For an object on the Earth's surface, the weight $mg$ *is* the gravitational attraction of the Earth, so

$$mg = G\frac{m M_E}{r_E^{2}}$$

The object's own mass appears on both sides and cancels, which is the algebraic reason all objects fall with the same acceleration. Solving for $g$ gives

$$g = \frac{G M_E}{r_E^{2}}$$

Substituting $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$, $M_E = 5.972 \times 10^{24}\ \text{kg}$ and $r_E = 6.38 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$ returns $9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$: the familiar figure is a consequence of the Earth's mass and radius, not a separate constant of nature.

## Far from the Earth's surface

As the distance from the Earth's centre increases, the gravitational force decreases, and so does the acceleration it produces. The same formula applies with the distance from the centre in place of the Earth's radius:

$$g_r = \frac{G M_E}{r^{2}}$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $g_r$ | The acceleration due to gravity at distance $r$ |
| $r_E$ | The radius of the Earth |
| $r$ | The distance from the Earth's centre |

Since the dependence is an inverse square in $r$, and $r$ is measured from the *centre*, climbing a few kilometres above the surface changes $r$ only very slightly from $r_E$ and so changes $g$ only very slightly. Gravity weakens with height, but not quickly — which is exactly why orbiting spacecraft, only a few hundred kilometres up, are still firmly held by the Earth.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Acceleration due to gravity at the surface** | $g = GM_E/r_E^2$, obtained by equating an object's weight to the Earth's gravitational attraction |
| **Acceleration due to gravity at a distance $r$** | $g_r = GM_E/r^2$, where $r$ is measured from the Earth's centre |

# 5.8 Satellites and "Weightlessness"

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Free fall and apparent weight

**Free fall** is the condition of an object falling with only gravity acting on it, without air resistance.

**Weightlessness** occurs when an astronaut in orbit feels weightless because both the shuttle and the astronaut are in free fall together. The quotation marks in the section title are doing real work: **the gravitational force is not zero**. There is no apparent weight only because there is no support force — the floor is falling away at exactly the rate the astronaut is falling, so it never pushes back.

What you feel as your weight is in fact the support force from whatever is holding you up. Remove the support while leaving gravity untouched, and the sensation of weight vanishes although the force has not.

## Orbits

A satellite in a circular orbit is held there by gravity, and gravity is therefore the source of the centripetal force. Equating the two,

$$\frac{G M m}{r^{2}} = \frac{m v^{2}}{r}$$

gives the **orbital speed**, in which the satellite's own mass has cancelled:

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$$

where $M$ is the mass of the central object and $r$ the radius of the orbit measured from its centre. The **orbital period** follows from the fact that one lap covers a circumference:

$$T = \frac{2\pi r}{v}$$

Because the satellite's mass cancels, a heavy satellite and a light one at the same altitude travel at the same speed with the same period — the same cancellation, and the same reason, as for objects in free fall at the surface.

## Worked example

*A satellite orbits Earth 225 km above its surface. The Earth's mass is $5.97 \times 10^{24}\ \text{kg}$ and its radius $6.38 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$. What are the satellite's orbital speed and period?*

The orbital radius is measured from the centre of the Earth, so the altitude must be added to the Earth's radius:

$$r = 6.38 \times 10^{6} + 2.25 \times 10^{5} = 6.605 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$$

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}} = \sqrt{\frac{(6.67 \times 10^{-11})(5.97 \times 10^{24})}{6.605 \times 10^{6}}} \approx 7.77 \times 10^{3}\ \text{m/s}$$

$$T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = \frac{2\pi (6.605 \times 10^{6})}{7.77 \times 10^{3}} \approx 5.3 \times 10^{3}\ \text{s}$$

which is about 89 minutes. Forgetting to add the altitude to the Earth's radius is the standard error in this calculation, and it gives an answer that looks plausible, so it is worth checking deliberately.

## Check your understanding

**What causes an object to stay in orbit around Earth?**

Gravity. It supplies the centripetal force that continuously turns the satellite's velocity toward the Earth, so the satellite keeps falling toward the Earth without ever getting closer to it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Free fall** | When an object is falling with only gravity acting on it, without air resistance |
| **Weightlessness** | The sensation experienced when an astronaut and the craft are in free fall together; the gravitational force is not zero, but there is no apparent weight because there is no support force |
| **Orbital speed** | $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$, where $M$ is the mass of the central object |
| **Orbital period** | $T = 2\pi r / v$, the time for one complete orbit |

# 5.9 Kepler's Laws and Newton's Synthesis

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Kepler's laws

Kepler's laws describe how planets actually move, and they were established from observation before there was any theory to explain them.

**First law.** Planets orbit the Sun in **elliptical** paths, with the Sun at one **focus**. Not at the centre — at a focus, which means a planet's distance from the Sun changes over the course of its year.

**Second law.** A line drawn from the Sun to a planet sweeps out **equal areas in equal time intervals**. Since the line is shorter when the planet is nearer the Sun, the planet must travel further along its orbit in a given time to sweep the same area, and so **planets move faster when they are closer to the Sun**. The law is a statement about speed disguised as a statement about area.

## Newton's synthesis

The orbital period and the orbital distance depend on the mass of the central object and the radius of the orbit, and **Kepler's third law can be derived using Newton's law** of universal gravitation.

The derivation is the same equation used for satellites in the previous section. Gravity supplies the centripetal force for a planet of mass $m$ in a circular orbit of radius $r$ about a central object of mass $M$:

$$\frac{GMm}{r^{2}} = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}$$

Substituting $v = 2\pi r/T$ and rearranging gives

$$T^{2} = \frac{4\pi^{2}}{GM}\,r^{3}$$

so $T^2$ is proportional to $r^3$, with a constant of proportionality that depends only on the mass of the central object — exactly the two dependencies stated above. Comparing two bodies orbiting the same central object, the constant cancels:

$$\frac{T_1^{2}}{T_2^{2}} = \frac{r_1^{3}}{r_2^{3}}$$

This is the synthesis: a law obtained from astronomical observation is shown to be a consequence of the same force that governs falling objects on Earth. The planets were not obeying a special rule of their own.

## Check your understanding

**Which of the following best explains why astronauts on the International Space Station feel weightless?**

Because the station and the astronauts are in free fall together, so nothing supports the astronauts and they have no apparent weight. It is not because gravity is absent at that altitude — gravity is what holds the station in orbit.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Kepler's first law** | Planets orbit the Sun in elliptical paths, with the Sun at one focus |
| **Kepler's second law** | A line drawn from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals; planets move faster when closer to the Sun |
| **Kepler's third law** | $T^2 \propto r^3$; the orbital period and distance depend on the mass of the central object and the radius of the orbit, and the relation is derivable from Newton's law of universal gravitation |

title: Work Done by a Constant Force
summary: Work is a scalar: the product of the magnitude of the displacement times the component of the force parallel to the displacement. W = F d \cos\theta where \theta is the angle between the force and the
markdown:
# 6.1 Work Done by a Constant Force

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What work is

**Work** is a scalar: the product of the magnitude of the displacement times the component of the force parallel to the displacement.

$$W = F d \cos\theta$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between the force and the displacement. Its unit is the **joule** (J).

The definition has two halves, and both matter. There must be a displacement, and the force must have a component along it. A force at right angles to the motion contributes nothing at all, because $\cos 90° = 0$ — the parallel component it needs to supply is zero.

Work is **positive** when the force and the displacement are in the same direction.

## Worked example

*A sailor pulls a boat a distance of 0.30 m along a dock using a rope that makes a 25.0° angle with the horizontal. How much work does the sailor do on the boat if he exerts a force of 255 N on the rope?*

The boat moves horizontally, but the rope pulls at 25.0° to the horizontal, so only the horizontal component of the 255 N does work:

$$W = Fd\cos\theta = 255 \times 0.30 \times \cos 25.0° \approx 69\ \text{J}$$

The same pattern — pulling a crate with a rope at an angle — recurs throughout the chapter.

## Lifting an object

Lifting an object vertically is the other standard case. Here the force is along the displacement, and the work done equals the change in gravitational potential energy of the object. This is the first sign of the connection developed in the rest of the chapter: work is the mechanism by which energy is transferred and stored.

## Check your understanding

**Which of the following results in zero work?**

A. Pushing a box across the floor
B. Holding a book without moving it
C. Pulling a sled in the snow
D. Dropping an object from a height

**Answer: B.** Holding a book takes force, but the book does not move, so the displacement is zero and $W = Fd\cos\theta = 0$. Effort is not work in the physics sense; work requires the point of application to move.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Work** | A scalar quantity: the product of the magnitude of the displacement times the component of the force parallel to the displacement, $W = Fd\cos\theta$ |
| **Joule (J)** | The unit of work |
| **Positive work** | Work done when force and displacement are in the same direction |

title: Work Done by a Varying Force
summary: W = Fd\cos\theta assumes a single value of F for the whole displacement. When the force changes with position, there is no single F to put in the formula, and work must be found another way: from the
markdown:
# 6.2 Work Done by a Varying Force

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Work as an area

$W = Fd\cos\theta$ assumes a single value of $F$ for the whole displacement. When the force changes with position, there is no single $F$ to put in the formula, and work must be found another way: **from the area under the force versus displacement curve.**

The work done is the area between the graph of $F$ and the $x$-axis, between the starting and finishing positions.

This is not a new definition of work but the same one applied piecewise. Over a displacement small enough that the force barely changes, the work is $F$ times that small displacement — the area of a thin strip under the curve. Adding the strips across the whole journey adds their areas, and the total is the area under the curve. The constant-force case is the special one where the graph is a horizontal line and the area is a rectangle, $F$ times $d$.

## Integration

In the limit of infinitely thin strips, that sum is an integral:

$$W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F\,dx$$

## Check your understanding

**What does the area under a Force versus Position graph represent?**

A. Velocity
B. Acceleration
C. Work
D. Power

**Answer: C.**

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Work done by a varying force** | The area between the force–displacement curve and the $x$-axis, $W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F\,dx$ |

markdown:
# 6.3 Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Principle

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Kinetic energy

**Kinetic energy** is the energy of motion:

$$KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$$

Like work, it is measured in joules, and like work it is a scalar — it carries no direction, so the sign of the velocity is irrelevant. An object moving left at $5\ \text{m/s}$ and one moving right at $5\ \text{m/s}$ have the same kinetic energy.

The dependence on $v^2$ means kinetic energy grows far faster than speed: doubling the speed of an object quadruples its kinetic energy.

## The work-energy principle

The **work-energy principle** states that the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy:

$$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_f^{2} - \tfrac{1}{2}mv_i^{2}$$

This is what makes work worth defining. It converts a question about forces and displacements into a question about speeds, without any of the intermediate detail about how the force varied along the way.

## Worked example

*A 145 g baseball is thrown so that it acquires a speed of 25 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?*

Convert the mass to kilograms first — $145\ \text{g} = 0.145\ \text{kg}$ — since the joule is built on kilograms, metres and seconds:

$$KE = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.145)(25)^{2} \approx 45\ \text{J}$$

## Check your understanding

**If net work on an object is positive, what happens to its kinetic energy?**

A. It decreases
B. It stays the same
C. It becomes zero
D. It increases

**Answer: D.** By the work-energy principle $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta KE$, so positive net work means a positive change in kinetic energy.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Kinetic energy (KE)** | The energy of motion, $KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ |
| **Work-energy principle** | The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy |

# 6.4 Potential Energy

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Stored energy

**Potential energy (PE)** is stored energy due to position. Two forms appear in this chapter:

| Form | Formula | Stored by |
|---|---|---|
| **Gravitational potential energy** | $PE = mgy$ | Raising a mass to a height $y$ |
| **Elastic (spring) potential energy** | $PE = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^{2}$ | Stretching or compressing a spring by $x$ from its natural length |

Here $k$ is the spring stiffness constant, in newtons per metre.

## The reference point

Potential energy is **relative to a chosen zero level**. There is no absolute height and therefore no absolute gravitational potential energy: you choose where $y = 0$, and every value of $PE$ in the problem is quoted with respect to that choice.

The choice is free, and different choices give different numbers for the *same* physical situation. What they never change is a **difference** in potential energy between two points, and it is always a difference that appears in physical predictions. So choose whatever zero makes the arithmetic easiest — usually the lowest point of the motion, or the starting point — and then use it consistently.

## Worked example: a roller-coaster car

*A 1000 kg roller-coaster car moves from point 1 to point 2 and then to point 3.*

**(a) Taking $y = 0$ at point 1**, the gravitational potential energy at points 2 and 3 is $mgy$ with each height measured from point 1. A point below the chosen zero has a negative height, and therefore a negative potential energy — which is perfectly acceptable, since only differences are physical.

**(b) The change in potential energy from point 2 to point 3** is the difference of the two values found in (a).

**(c) Repeating with $y = 0$ at point 3** gives $PE = 0$ at point 3 by definition, and different numbers at points 1 and 2. But the change in potential energy from point 2 to point 3 comes out the same as in (b). That is the lesson of the example: the reference point moves all the individual values up or down together, and cancels out of every difference.

## Worked example: a spring

*A spring has a spring stiffness constant of 440 N/m. How much must this spring be stretched to store 25 J of potential energy?*

Rearranging $PE = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$ for $x$:

$$x = \sqrt{\frac{2\,PE}{k}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 25}{440}} \approx 0.34\ \text{m}$$

## Check your understanding

**Which of the following increases an object's gravitational potential energy?**

A. Lowering it to the ground
B. Compressing a spring
C. Raising it to a higher shelf
D. Sliding it on a level surface

**Answer: C.** Gravitational potential energy is $mgy$, so it increases only when $y$ increases. Compressing a spring stores energy, but elastic potential energy, not gravitational.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Potential energy (PE)** | Stored energy due to position |
| **Gravitational potential energy** | $PE = mgy$, the energy stored by raising a mass to a height |
| **Elastic (spring) potential energy** | $PE = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$, the energy stored by stretching or compressing a spring |
| **Spring stiffness constant ($k$)** | The constant, in N/m, measuring how stiff a spring is |
| **Reference point** | The chosen zero level with respect to which potential energy is measured |

# 6.5 Conservative and Nonconservative Forces

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The distinction

A **conservative force** is one for which the work done is **path-independent**: it depends only on the starting and finishing points, not on the route taken between them. Gravity is the standard example.

A **nonconservative force** is one for which the work done **depends on the path**. Friction is the standard example — the longer the route, the more work friction does against the motion, even if the object ends up in the same place.

| | Conservative | Nonconservative |
|---|---|---|
| Work done | Path-independent | Depends on the path |
| Example | Gravity | Friction |
| Potential energy | Can be defined | Cannot be defined |

## Identifying which type a force is

The test is the last row of that table: **if a potential energy can be defined for a force, the force is conservative.**

The reason follows from the previous section. Potential energy is a function of *position* alone — $mgy$ depends on where the object is and nothing else. For such a quantity to describe the work a force does, that work must itself depend only on the positions at the two ends of the journey. A force whose work depends on the route taken cannot be summarised by any function of position, so no potential energy exists for it.

## Mechanical energy and friction

*A box sliding down a ramp with friction loses mechanical energy due to friction.*

This is what the distinction costs in practice. Gravity does work on the box that can be fully accounted for as a change in gravitational potential energy, and recovered if the box goes back up. The work done against friction cannot be recovered: it is not stored anywhere as potential energy, and the mechanical energy of the box is reduced by it.

## Check your understanding

**Which of the following is a conservative force?**

A. Friction
B. Tension
C. Gravity
D. Air resistance

**Answer: C.** Gravity has a potential energy, $mgy$, defined for it; friction and air resistance both do path-dependent work.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Conservative force** | A force whose work is path-independent, such as gravity |
| **Nonconservative force** | A force whose work depends on the path taken, such as friction |

# 8.1 Angular Quantities

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Rotation needs its own set of quantities, because every point of a rotating body travels a different distance at a different speed while the body as a whole turns by one definite amount. The angular quantities describe the turning itself.

## Angular position and displacement

**Angular position** $\theta$ is the angle an object has rotated relative to a reference line. Its unit is the **radian** (rad), defined by

$$\theta = \frac{s}{r}$$

where $s$ is the arc length in metres and $r$ the radius in metres. A radian is thus the angle for which the arc length equals the radius; being a ratio of two lengths, it is a pure number, which is why radians can be multiplied into linear quantities without carrying a unit along.

Rotation has a sign convention, as straight-line motion does:

| Direction | Sign |
|---|---|
| Counterclockwise | Positive |
| Clockwise | Negative |

## Converting between degrees and radians

A full turn is $360°$ and also $2\pi$ radians, so the two units are related by $180° = \pi\ \text{rad}$:

$$\text{degrees} \to \text{radians:}\quad \theta_{\text{rad}} = \theta_{\deg} \times \frac{\pi}{180}$$

$$\text{radians} \to \text{degrees:}\quad \theta_{\deg} = \theta_{\text{rad}} \times \frac{180}{\pi}$$

## Angular velocity

**Angular velocity** $\omega$ is the rate of change of angular displacement over time:

$$\omega = \frac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t}$$

measured in radians per second (rad/s). It takes the same sign convention: counterclockwise positive, clockwise negative.

Its properties are read off a graph of angular position against time, exactly as velocity is read off a position–time graph in straight-line motion:

- **Constant $\omega$**: the graph of $\theta$ against time is a straight line.
- **Changing $\omega$**: the graph of $\theta$ is curved, and the slope of the tangent at a point gives the instantaneous $\omega$ at that moment.

## Relationship between linear and angular quantities

A point at distance $r$ from the axis moves along an arc of length $s = r\theta$, so dividing by the time taken gives its linear speed:

$$v = r\omega$$

This single relation is the bridge between the two descriptions, and it says something that is easy to get wrong: the angular velocity belongs to the *whole rotating body*, while the linear speed belongs to a *particular point on it* and grows with distance from the axis.

## Check your understanding

**Two points, A and B, are on a rotating disk, with B farther from the centre. Which point has a greater angular velocity? Which has a greater linear velocity? Why?**

The disk is rigid, so both points sweep through the same angle in the same time: their **angular velocities are equal**. But $v = r\omega$, and B has the larger $r$, so **B has the greater linear velocity** — it has a longer circle to travel in the same time.

**Convert 2.5 radians into degrees.**

$$2.5 \times \frac{180}{\pi} \approx 143°$$

**Convert 135° into radians.**

$$135 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{3\pi}{4} \approx 2.36\ \text{rad}$$

**The Earth completes one full rotation in 24 hours. What is its angular velocity in rad/s?**

One full rotation is $2\pi$ rad and 24 hours is $86\,400\ \text{s}$, so

$$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{86\,400} \approx 7.3 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{rad/s}$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Angular position ($\theta$)** | The angle an object has rotated relative to a reference line, $\theta = s/r$ |
| **Radian (rad)** | The unit of angular position, defined as the arc length divided by the radius |
| **Arc length ($s$)** | The distance measured along the circular path, in metres |
| **Angular velocity ($\omega$)** | The rate of change of angular displacement over time, $\omega = \Delta\theta/\Delta t$, in rad/s |

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Physics H review guide (PA). Writers: Aryana Xu 9-1, Leyi Lian 9-5. Editor: Lucas 9-3. Range: Chapters 2-4. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

-Mechanics: study of motion and force

**Reference Frames**

-Motion: an object changes position relative to a reference frame (or reference point)

-Reference frame: a place or object used for comparison to determine something is/is not in motion. It is assumed to be stationary.

-Motion diagram: series of images showing the positions of a moving object at equal time intervals. Its purpose is to visualize displacement and velocity.

-Particle model: simplified version of motion diagram, which the object in motion is replaced by dots.

For example: every dot is after a unit of time has passed

Speed up: . . . .

Slow down: . . . .

Constant speed: . . . .

At Rest: .

-Vectors: quantities with a direction (defined by + or – symbol) and magnitude

e.g. displacement, velocity, force

(remember to define direction)

-Scalars: quantities with magnitude but no direction

e.g. distance, speed, temperature

**Average Velocity**

-Speed: the rate an object moves, the distance the object travels per unit of time SCALAR

Speed=Distance/Time Average Speed=Total Distance/Total Time Unit: m/s

-Velocity: speed with direction, represented by the + or – symbol VECTOR

Velocity=Displacement/Time Average Velocity=Total Displacement/Time Unit: m/s

-Uniform motion: motion in a straight line with constant velocity

**Instantaneous Velocity**

-Instantaneous velocity (/speed): the velocity (/speed) at any instant of time

Magnitude of instantaneous velocity=instantaneous speed

**Please note that PA materials are student-created and for reference only.**

-in constant speed, the instantaneous and average speed is the same

**Acceleration**

-Acceleration: the rate at which object’s velocity changes

Acceleration=Change of Velocity/Time=(Vfinal-Vinitial)/Time Unit: m/s²

-Moving to “+” direction, speeding up: Positive a

-Moving to “+” direction, slowing down: Negative a

-Moving to “-” direction, speeding up: Negative a

-Moving to “-” direction, slowing down: Positive a

-both Vinitial’s direction and +/- Acceleration determines speed up or slow down

**Motion at Constant Acceleration**

-Uniformly Accelerated Motion: motion with constant acceleration

-Acceleration has constant magnitude + same direction

Circular motion does NOT belong to motion at Constant Acceleration because the acceleration has different directions

Instantaneous Acceleration = Average Acceleration

**Motion Not at Constant Acceleration**

How to Find:

-Average Acceleration: Connect A and B on the graph, find the slope of the line

Average Acceleration=(Velocity B-Velocity A)/Time=Slope

-Instantaneous Acceleration: Find the slope of the tangent line of A

-When time is closer to 0, the Average and Instantaneous Acceleration gets closer values

**Special Formulas**

- Velocity Final = Velocity Initial + Acceleration*Time
- Displacement = (Velocity Initial + Velocity Final)*Time/2
- Displacement = Velocity Initial*Time + (Aceleration*Time²)/2
- Displacement = (Velocity final² - Velocity initial²)/2*Acceleration

**Please note that PA materials are student-created and for reference only.**

**Falling Objects**

-Free Fall: motion of a falling object when air resistance is negligible, and the action can be considered due to gravity alone

-Galileo’s Hypothesis: At a given location on the earth and in the absence of air resistance, all objects fall with the same constant acceleration

Gravitational Acceleration on earth: g=9.8 m/s² toward the center of earth

1.Position-Time Graph (d-t graph)

When v=0 (no motion) When v=constant (uniform motion)

-Horizontal straight line, parallel to t-axis -Slanted straight line

-y-intercept: initial position

-Intersection: two objects meet

-Slope: average velocity

Constant Acceleration

-Made up by many straight-line segments

Varying Acceleration

-Curve graph line

-Average velocity: slope of connection of two dots on the line

-Instantaneous velocity: slope of tangent to a point on a curve

2.Velocity-Time Graph (v-t graph)

When v=0 (No motion) When v=constant (Uniform motion)

-Slope=0, instantaneous acceleration=0

-Horizontal line

-Displacement: area formed by the graph line and t-axis

-Two objects meet when they have the same area

Uniformly Accelerated Motion

-Slanted straight line

-Slope=average acceleration=instantaneous acceleration

Motion with Changing Acceleration

-Instantaneous acceleration: slope of the tangent to the curve for a particular moment

3.Acceleration-Time Graph (a-t graph)

Uniformly Accelerated Motion

-Horizontal line parallel to t-axis

-Area below line and t-axis is the change of velocity

Changing Acceleration Motion

# S1M-3 Chapter 4: Dynamics: Newton’s Laws of Motion

## Chapter 4: Dynamics: Newton’s Laws of Motion

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Physics H review guide (PA). Writers: Aryana Xu 9-1, Leyi Lian 9-5. Editor: Lucas 9-3. Range: Chapters 2-4. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**Force**

-Force: a push or pull exerted by one object on another. Force is a vector

-System: to whom the force is exerted

Agent: by whom the force is exerted

-The effect of a force: 1) to cause a deformation: a change in dimension/ shape

2) to change the state of motion: change velocity

-Unit: Newton (N). I N= 1kg m/s2

-Measurement device: Spring scale

The larger the force, the spring is stretched longer, hence larger reading

-3 factors of Force

Magnitude: the strength of the force vector

Direction: in which direction the force vector acts

Point of application: the location the force is exerted

-Graphical representation: line segment with an arrow

**Types of Forces**

-4 fundamental forces: Gravitational force, electromagnetic force, strong force, weak force

-Contact force: an object from the external world touches a system and thereby exerts a force on it

e.g. friction, drag force (air resistance/ fluid resistance), tension, normal force, spring force, applied force

These are non-fundamental forces, and are instead consequences of fundamental forces

-Field force: exerted without contact

e.g. gravitational force, electric force, magnetic force

-Spring force: Fsp=-kx

Fsp: force exerted by the spring on the attached object (N)

x: the displacement of the spring end from its equilibrium position (cm)

k: spring constant (N/cm)

- : F is opposite to x

-Hooke’s law: the magnitude of the force is directly proportional to the amount of stretch or compression within the limit of a spring

-Elastic limit: point beyond which the spring will no longer return to its original shape when the force is removed

**Friction**

-Sliding friction: occurs when 2 solid surfaces slide over each other

Static friction (Ffs): caused by tendency of relative motion, where there is no relative motion between 2 objects in touch

Kinetic friction (Ffk): caused by relative motion between 2 objects in touch

-Rolling friction: occurs when an object rolls over a surface. Rolling friction is smaller than sliding friction

-Fluid friction: occurs when an object move through a fluid

e.g. air resistance/ friction in water/ oil

-Air resistance depends on 4 factors

1) shape of object. Streamline reduce friction

2) size of object. Air resistance increases when surface area increases

3) speed of object. Air resistance increases when speed increases

4) fluid type/ viscosity. Air resistance increases when fluid is more viscous

**Formulas for Friction**

-Ffs= Fcause

-Ffs max= μs Fn

fs max: maximum static friction

μs: coefficient of static friction, increased when surface is rougher

FN: normal force between 2 surfaces

Range of fs: 0<fs≤fs max

-Ffk= μk FN

μk: coefficient of kinetic friction, does not change with Fcause

Ffk: kinetic friction

FN: normal force

-μs≥ μk

-Coefficients of friction can also >1

**Balanced Forces**

-Equilibrium state: at rest or uniform motion, Fnet=0

-balanced forces: 2 forces on the same line on the same object that add up to 0

-Unbalanced forces: net force ≠ 0

Consequences: start/ stop moving, change direction. Unbalanced forces will change object’s motion

-Judge if 3 forces can be balanced or not: can/ cannot form triangle

**Newton’s First Law of Motion**

-Statement: every object continues in its state of rest, or of uniform velocity in a straight line, as long as no net force acts on it

-Also called law of inertia

-Inertia: tendency of an object to maintain its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line

Inertia is not a force. The greater the mass, the greater the inertia

-In accelerating frame of reference, Newton’s first law does not hold

-Inertial reference frames: reference frames in which Newton’s first law does hold

A reference frame moving with constant v relative to an IRF is also an IRF

e.g. Earth/ ground can be seen as an inertial reference frame

-Noninertial reference frames: reference frames in which the law of inertia does not hold

**Mass**

-Inertial mass: mass is equal to the ratio of the net force exerted on an object to its acceleration

-Mass is a measure of inertia of an object

-Formula: minertial = Fnet/ a

-Gravitational mass: mass as used in the law of universal gravitation determines the size of the gravitational force between 2 objects

-Formula: mgrav= r2Fgrav/ Gm

-Principle of Equivalence: Newton- inertial mass and gravitational mass are equal in magnitude

**Newton’s Second Law of Motion**

-Statement: the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it, and is inversely proportional to its mass. The direction of the acceleration is in the direction of the net force acting on the object

-Formula: ΣF= ma

ΣF: vector sum of all forces

-Unit: Newton

**Apparent weight**

-A spring scale measures weight, not mass

-Apparent weight: the force exerted by the scale

-Scenarios in an elevator:

1. Equilibrium: Fsp= Fg

2. Uniform acceleration upward: Fnet= Fsp- Fg, Fsp> Fg

Apparent weight> actual weight: overweight

3. Uniform acceleration downward: Fnet= Fg- Fsp, Fsp< Fg

Apparent weight< Actual weight

4. Elevator in Free fall: Fnet= Fg- Fsp= 0, Fsp= 0

Apparent weight= 0: Weightlessness

Weightlessness: no contact forces pushing up on the object, which makes its apparent weight 0. The object’s actual weight is not 0.

# S1MPA-1 Chapter 2: Motion

## Chapter 2: Motion

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm (PA) Physics H review guide (PA). Writers: Tianyuan 9(6), Dash 9(11). Editor: Serena 9(6). Range: Chapter 2-4. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

### 2.1–2.4: Foundations of Motion

**Reference frame:** an object used for comparison when measuring **position**, **distance or speed**.

**Particle model:** a simplified motion diagram in which the moving object is replaced by a **series of particles (dots)**, showing the object's position at **equal time intervals**.

**a) Vector vs. scalar**

**Vector: magnitude and direction**

- Position (vector): location of an object in a coordinate plane.
- Displacement (vector): change in position of an object ($\Delta d = d_f - d_i$).
- Velocity (vector): speed with both magnitude and direction.
- Acceleration (vector): rate at which velocity changes.

**Scalar: magnitude only**

- Distance (scalar): total length travelled by an object.
- Speed (scalar): distance travelled per unit of time.

**b) Velocity and acceleration: basic formulas**

- Average velocity: $\bar v = \frac{\Delta d}{\Delta t}$
- Instantaneous velocity: $v = \frac{\Delta d}{\Delta t}$ with $\Delta t$ infinitely close to 0
- Average acceleration: $\bar a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$
- Instantaneous acceleration: $a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$ with $\Delta t$ infinitely close to 0

### 2.5–2.6: Motion at Constant Acceleration

**Definition:** **uniformly accelerated motion** = motion with constant acceleration (the acceleration doesn't change).

**The 5 core kinematic formulas (very important):**

1. $a = \frac{V_f - V_i}{t}$
2. $V_f = V_i + at$
3. $d = V_it + \frac{at^2}{2}$
4. $d = \frac{(V_i + V_f)\,t}{2}$
5. $d = \frac{V_f^2 - V_i^2}{2a}$

**Problem-solving strategy:**

1. List the known variables (e.g. $V_i$, $V_f$, $a$, $t$, $\Delta d$) and mark the direction.
2. Choose the formula that contains the 3 knowns and 1 unknown.

### 2.7: Falling Objects

**a) Free fall**

- **Definition:** the motion of a falling object when **air resistance is negligible** and the motion is **due to gravity** alone.
- **Galileo's hypothesis:** at a given location on Earth, in the absence of air resistance, **all objects fall with the same constant acceleration** (regardless of mass).
- **Acceleration due to gravity:** $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$, directed toward the centre of the Earth.

> Object dropped: $V_i = 0$ m/s; object thrown down: $V_i \ne 0$ m/s. Use $+g$ when downward is positive and $-g$ when upward is positive.

**b) Motion when thrown up** (upward taken as +)

1. The **magnitude** of gravity always stays the same ($g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$).
2. $V_i$ is (+), initial $\Delta d = 0$.
3. **Highest position:** $V = 0$, and $\Delta d$ is largest in the (+) direction.
4. **Above** the initial position: $\Delta d$ is (+); **below** the initial position: $\Delta d$ is (−).
5. **Rising:** $V$ (+), $\Delta d$ (+). **Falling:** $V$ (−), $\Delta d$ (+) above the start or $\Delta d$ (−) below it.
6. For the **same $\Delta d$**, the **speed is the same** (in opposite directions).
7. On returning to the **initial position**: $V = -V_i$, $\Delta d = 0$, and $t_{rise} = t_{fall}$.

### 2.8: Graphical Analysis of Linear Motion

Three major graphs for motion: position–time (d–t), velocity–time (v–t) and acceleration–time (a–t).

**a) Position–time graph (d–t)**

1. **No motion (at rest):** a horizontal straight line, parallel to the x-axis.
2. **Uniform motion (constant v):**
   - a slanted straight line;
   - y-intercept = initial position;
   - where two lines intersect, the two objects meet;
   - since velocity is constant, instantaneous velocity = average velocity ($v = \frac{d}{t}$);
   - **slope = average velocity** ($v = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}$).
3. **Accelerated motion:**
   - (a) many straight segments: an instant change in velocity at each corner;
   - (b) a curved line (parabola): **average velocity** = slope of the chord connecting two points on the parabola; **instantaneous velocity** = slope of the tangent line at that moment.

**Relationships between displacement, velocity and acceleration** (from the d–t curve's shape):

| Curve | Signs | Motion |
|---|---|---|
| rising, getting steeper | $d > 0,\ v > 0,\ a > 0$ | speeding up ($v$, $a$ both +) |
| falling, getting steeper | $d > 0,\ v < 0,\ a < 0$ | speeding up ($v$, $a$ both −) |
| falling, levelling off | $d > 0,\ v < 0,\ a > 0$ | slowing down ($v$, $a$ different signs) |
| rising, levelling off | $d > 0,\ v > 0,\ a < 0$ | slowing down ($v$, $a$ different signs) |

**b) Velocity–time graph (v–t)**

1. **Uniform motion ($a = 0$):**
   - **horizontal line:** $v$ = constant, $a = 0$;
   - the **y-axis** gives the velocity at any moment directly; the sign gives the direction: (+) above the x-axis, (−) below.
2. **Uniformly accelerated motion:**
   - a slanted straight line;
   - slope = acceleration = $\frac{V_f - V_i}{t}$ (average = instantaneous, since $a$ is constant);
   - **rising line:** $a > 0$; **descending line:** $a < 0$; **steeper:** larger $|a|$.
3. **Changing acceleration:**
   - **curved line:** instantaneous $a$ = slope of the tangent at that moment. For example, a curve rising ever more steeply means speed increasing with $v$ (+) and $a$ (+) increasing; a curve rising and levelling off means speed increasing with $a$ (+) decreasing.

**Area between the graph line and the x-axis = displacement.**

- Area above the x-axis: $\Delta d > 0$; below: $\Delta d < 0$.
- Displacement = (positive-direction area) − (negative-direction area), i.e. $A_1 - A_2$.
- Two objects meet when they have the same area (not when their lines cross).

**c) Acceleration–time graph (a–t)**

- **Uniformly accelerated motion:** a horizontal line parallel to the x-axis.
- Area under the a–t graph = change in velocity ($\Delta v = at$).

**d) Graph conversion (d–t ⇄ v–t ⇄ a–t)**

- **d to v:** the slope of d–t gives v–t.
- **v to d:** the area under v–t gives the displacement for d–t.
- **v to a:** the slope of v–t gives a–t.
- **a to v:** the area under a–t gives $\Delta v$.
- **Curves:** use the relationships table above.
- **Corners:** sudden changes in displacement and velocity appear as $\pm\infty$ spikes on the a–t graph.

# S1MPA-2 Chapter 3

## Chapter 3

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm (PA) Physics H review guide (PA). Writers: Tianyuan 9(6), Dash 9(11). Editor: Serena 9(6). Range: Chapter 2-4. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

### 3.1 Vectors and Scalars

**Vectors** have magnitude and direction, e.g. velocity, displacement, force. Vectors with the same magnitude but different directions are not equal.

**Scalars** have ONLY magnitude, no direction, e.g. speed, distance, temperature.

> Some problems ask for ONLY the magnitude of a vector.

**Velocity, speed, displacement and distance:**

- Displacement is the length from the starting point to the ending point. Velocity = displacement / time. In one motion, displacement is less than or equal to distance.
- Distance is the length of the path the object travelled. Speed = distance / time.

**How to draw one vector:**

1. Draw a coordinate plane with x and y axes, and label the axes (x, y or N, S, E, W).
2. Draw a scale with a 1 cm segment (recommended) and label the scale ratio.
3. Measure and label the angle of the vector to show the direction.
4. Draw to scale, unit by unit, to show the magnitude.
5. Draw an arrow (you can label the vector's magnitude).
6. Write the final vector (away from the labelled arrow) with magnitude and direction, e.g. $\vec R = 3$ m/s @ 30° above horizontal.

**Reminders:**

1. Every vector's magnitude should span AT LEAST 2 units.
2. The arrowhead should not go past the labelled unit.
3. The vector's tail should start from the origin.
4. DON'T FORGET TO LABEL!!!

**Notation:** final answer $\vec R = n$ (unit) $m^\circ$ A of B. Ways to express angles:

1. $m^\circ$ above / below horizontal (often when working with x and y);
2. $m^\circ$ N of W, or other directions (meaning $m^\circ$ toward N starting from W);
3. $m^\circ$ (U, D, L, R) of (+x, +y, −x, −y) (rare: $m^\circ$ from that axis in that direction).

### 3.2 Addition of Vectors: Graphical Methods

**Resultant** ($\vec R$ or $(\text{unit})_R$): the sum of two or more vectors. For magnitudes $v_1 \ge v_2$, the magnitude of the resultant satisfies $v_1 - v_2 \le v_R \le v_1 + v_2$.

The resultant can be smaller than the individual vectors, e.g. when the vectors point in opposite directions.

**Adding vectors by graphing (triangle method):**

1. Draw a coordinate plane (if needed) and a scale (see above).
2. Draw and label the first vector in its given direction and magnitude, with its tail at the origin.
3. Draw and label the second vector with its tail starting from the first vector's tip.
4. Repeat step 3 for any further vectors.
5. Draw the resultant from the origin to the final vector's tip.
6. Measure and label the resultant's length and direction using a ruler and protractor.
7. Calculate the final magnitude using the scale and write the final answer (e.g. $\Delta d_R \approx 3.7\text{ cm} \times \frac{2\text{ m}}{1\text{ cm}} \approx 7.4$ m, so $\Delta \vec d_R \approx 7.4$ m @ 57° N of E).

**Adding vectors by graphing (parallelogram method):** uncommon (check the question's requirements), and used with only two vectors.

1. Repeat steps 1 to 3 of the triangle method.
2. Draw and label the second vector again from the origin (the first vector's tail).
3. Draw and label the first vector again from the second vector's tip.
4. The result is a parallelogram: draw the resultant as the diagonal from the origin.
5. Repeat steps 6 to 7 of the triangle method.

**Special cases:**

1. **The resultant equals 0:** two or more vectors placed tip to tail form a closed shape, so there is no gap between the first and last vector.
2. **The vectors point in opposite directions:** one may be longer than the other, so they overlap when graphed. Label each with a brace "{" and leave space between them to tell them apart.

**Calculation method** (only for two perpendicular vectors):

1. Graph using the triangle method if the question requires a graph.
2. Define the positive directions (often two).
3. Use the Pythagorean Theorem to calculate the resultant's magnitude (the hypotenuse).
4. Use trigonometry to calculate the angle of the resultant's direction.
5. Write the final resultant with magnitude and direction.

### 3.3 Subtraction of Vectors, Multiplication of Vectors by a Scalar

**Negative vectors:** two vectors with the same magnitude but exactly opposite directions.

$$A - B = A + (-B)$$

**Graphing subtraction of vectors:** since $\vec v_1 = \vec v_R + \vec v_2$, we have $\vec v_R = \vec v_1 - \vec v_2$.

1. Place the vectors tail to tail, because $\vec v_2$ should connect $\vec v_1$ and $\vec v_R$.
2. Connect the first vector's tip to the second vector's tip and label it as the resultant.
3. Graph it and write the answer as shown before.

**Multiplying vectors by scalars:** $\vec A \times c$. If the scalar $c$ is negative, the answer's direction reverses.

1. Calculate the answer for the given vector and scalar.
2. Graph it directly (if required) as before.

### 3.4 Adding Vectors by Components

Vectors on a coordinate plane can be broken into horizontal and vertical components.

**Vector resolution:** separating and combining components using trigonometry ($\vec A = \vec A_x + \vec A_y$), where $\sin\theta = \frac{A_y}{A}$ and $\cos\theta = \frac{A_x}{A}$.

**Separating a vector:**

- $A_x = A\cos\theta$ gives the x component of a vector.
- $A_y = A\sin\theta$ gives the y component.

**Combining components:**

- $A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$ gives the magnitude (from the Pythagorean theorem).
- $\theta = \arctan\left(\frac{A_y}{A_x}\right)$ gives the direction relative to the x-axis ($\tan^{-1}$ on a calculator).

**Solving for a resultant by vector resolution:**

1. Define the positive directions (often one on each axis).
2. Separate the given vectors into components, noting positive and negative directions (draw it if you need to).
3. Sum the components on each axis, keeping track of signs.
4. Solve for the resultant's magnitude and direction using the combining formulas.
5. Write the final resultant as shown previously.

**Worked example** (N and E positive): $\vec A_1 = 50$ m @ 30° N of E, $\vec A_2 = 100$ m @ 60° N of W.

- $A_{1x} = 50\cos 30^\circ = 25\sqrt{3}$ m (E); $A_{1y} = 50\sin 30^\circ = 25$ m (N)
- $A_{2x} = 100\cos 60^\circ = 50$ m (W); $A_{2y} = 100\sin 60^\circ = 50\sqrt{3}$ m (N)
- $A_x = (25\sqrt{3} - 50)$ m $\approx -6.7$ m; $A_y = (25 + 50\sqrt{3})$ m $\approx 111.6$ m
- $A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2} \approx 111.8$ m; $\theta = \arctan\left(\left|\frac{A_y}{A_x}\right|\right) \approx 86.5^\circ$, so $\vec A \approx 111.8$ m @ 86.5° N of W

### 3.5 & 3.6 Projectile Motion

- **Projectile:** an object shot through the air.
- **Trajectory:** the curved flight path the projectile travels.
- **Projectile motion:** the combination of two independent, perpendicular motions:
  - horizontal motion: constant velocity (no air resistance);
  - vertical motion: constant acceleration ($g$, gravitational acceleration).
- **Important assumptions:** no contact forces during flight and no air resistance. Therefore $v_{fx} = v_{ix}$, and horizontal motion can use $d = vt$. The velocity is always tangent to the trajectory.

**Maximum height** ($H_{max}$): the highest point the projectile reaches (where $v_y = 0$).

**Level horizontal range** ($R$): horizontal distance travelled when the start and end heights are the same ($\Delta y = 0$). Two complementary launch angles (with the same initial speed) give the same $R$.

**Flight time / hang time** ($t_{flight}$): the time the projectile spends in the air.

**Formulas:**

- $d_x = v_{ix}t$: horizontal distance within a time.
- $h_{max} = \frac{v_{iy}^2}{2g}$: maximum height relative to the initial height, derived from $d = \frac{v_f^2 - v_i^2}{2a}$.
- $t_{highest} = \frac{v_{iy}}{g}$: time to reach the maximum height from the initial position.
- $t_{total} = \frac{2v_{iy}}{g}$: flight time, ONLY WHEN $\Delta y = 0$.
- $R = v_{ix} \times t_{flight} = \frac{v_i^2\sin 2\theta_i}{g}$: level horizontal range, derived from the formulas above.
- $v_f = \sqrt{v_{fy}^2 + v_{ix}^2}$: magnitude of the final velocity before hitting the ground.
- $\theta = \arctan\left(\frac{v_{fy}}{v_{fx}}\right)$: direction of the final velocity before hitting the ground.

**Pro tips:**

- Defining a positive direction keeps your calculations clear.
- If $\Delta y = 0$, use the range formula. If not, use the $d_x$ formula and solve for the total time.
- Use the other kinematic equations for unknown parts; take care to plug in the correct numbers.
- To find the velocity at a moment, use $v_f = v_i + at$ to solve for $v_y$.
- Simplify the question by noting what information is given and what is needed.

### 3.8 Relative Velocity

**Relative velocity:** the velocity of one body relative to another. $\vec v_{AB}$ means the velocity of object A from object B's perspective.

**Basic formulas:**

- $\vec v_{AB} = -\vec v_{BA}$: e.g. when you run past a person, you see them moving backward, and vice versa.
- $\vec v_{AC} = \vec v_{AB} + \vec v_{BC}$: e.g. when you run on a bus, your velocity relative to the road is the sum of your velocity relative to the bus and the bus's velocity.

Questions in one dimension are usually just addition and subtraction.

**Relative velocity in two dimensions** (wind / current problems): if the wind is perpendicular to the motion, use the Pythagorean theorem.

- If the wind is not perpendicular, separate it into components and use vector resolution; these questions work like vector resolution.

**Other problems:** use the two basic formulas to convert between frames and get the final answer, with trigonometry where needed.

# S1MPA-3 Chapter 4: Newton's Laws of Motion

## Chapter 4: Newton's Laws of Motion

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm (PA) Physics H review guide (PA). Writers: Tianyuan 9(6), Dash 9(11). Editor: Serena 9(6). Range: Chapter 2-4. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

### 4.1 & 4.6 Force

- **Force:** a push or pull exerted by one object on another; a vector, unit N ($\text{kg·m/s}^2$).
- **Contact force:** exerted when two things touch.
- **Field force:** exerted without contact (e.g. gravity).
- **3 factors of a force:** magnitude, direction, point of application.
- An ***agent*** applies a force to a ***system***.
- **4 fundamental forces:** gravitational, electromagnetic, strong and weak.

**Hooke's law:** $F_{sp} = -kx$, where $F$ is the spring force, $k$ the spring constant and $x$ the change in the spring's length compared with its original length. On an F–x graph the extension is directly proportional to the force, up to the **elastic limit**: the point beyond which the spring no longer returns to its original shape when the force is removed.

**Friction:**

- **Sliding friction:**
  - static friction: $F_{fs,\max} = \mu_sF_n$;
  - kinetic friction: $F_{fk} = \mu_kF_n$, with $F_{fk} \le F_{fs,\max}$. (On a force–time graph, friction rises with the applied force until the object slides, then drops to the constant kinetic value.)
- **Rolling friction.**
- **Fluid friction:** e.g. air resistance, friction in water.

**Air resistance factors:**

- shape: streamlining reduces friction;
- size: larger area, more friction;
- speed: faster, more friction;
- viscosity: more viscous, more friction.

**Balanced forces:** two forces acting on the same object with the same magnitude and opposite directions.

### 4.2 Newton's First Law

1. Every object continues in its state of motion until a net force acts on it.
2. **Inertia** is the tendency of an object to maintain its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line (more mass, more inertia).

> The first law only applies in an inertial reference frame!

**Free-body diagram tips:**

- the normal force is perpendicular to the surface;
- gravity always points down;
- friction acts opposite to the object's motion;
- static friction exists whenever an object has a tendency to move (e.g. pressing an eraser against a wall, there is still upward static friction on the eraser).

# S1F-1 Chapter 1: Introduction, Measurement, Estimating

## Chapter 1: Introduction, Measurement, Estimating

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Final Physics H review guide (PA). Writers: Aryana Xu 9-1, Sharon Ren 9-3. Editor: Atticus Lee 9-6. Range: Chapter 1& Chapter 4. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 1.4 Measurement and Uncertainty; Significant Figures

-Measurement: comparison between an unknown quantity and a standard

-More significant figures: more precise

-Significant digits: the valid/ reliable digits in a measurement

-Estimated/ uncertain digit: last digit in a measurement

**Rules for Counting Significant Digits**

- All nonzero digits and any zeros contained between nonzero digits count

300042: 6 significant digits

- Exact numbers have an infinite number of significant digits

60 pages: infinite significant digits

- Leading zeros do not count

0.000034: 2 significant digits

- Trailing zeros count if there is a decimal point

0.0002500: 4 significant digits

- Trailing zeros may or may not count if there is no decimal point

190000: 2 significant digits

- In scientific notation, only count the term- the power does not count

1.9* 105 km: 2 significant digits

-Scientific notation: a* 10n, where a is between 1 and 10, and n is an integer

**Calculations with** **significant digits**

-The result never can be more precise than the least- precise measurement

-Use all digits throughout calculations, only round off answers to the appropriate significant digits (calulate the answers first, then round the answer)

-Addition/ subtraction: round the result to have as many decimal places as the measured number with the smallest number of decimal places.

-Multiplication/ division: round the result to have as many significant figures as the measured number with the smallest number of significant figures

**Uncertainty**

-Uncertainty: the variation in measured data

-No measurement made is ever exact

-Accuracy: how close a measurement is to the accepted value

-Precision: the repeatability of the measurements using a given instrument, increases with the number of significant figures

**Error**

-Random errors: statistical fluctuations in either direction in the measured data due to the precision limitations of the measurement device

-Random errors can be reduced by averaging over a large number of observations

-Least count: smallest division that is marked on the instrument

-Instrument Limit of Error (ILE): 1/2 of least count in analogue reading device, least count in digital reading device

-Deviation: repeat measurement several times, find average and then deviation

-Systematic errors: reproducible inaccuracies that are consistently in the same direction. The result of a mis- calibrated device, or a measuring technique which always makes the measured value larger or smaller than the true value

-Example: wrongly calibrated scale; using steel ruler at very low/ high temperature, in low temperature overestimate, in high temperature underestimate; reaction time of experimenter in stopwatches; zero error

-Systematic errors cannot be detected/ reduced by repeating measurements

-For each physics quantity, choose the largest of ILE, deviation, systematic error for uncertainty

-Uncertainty: 1 significant figure, in the same place as measured value’s last significant figure

-(Measured value + uncertainty) unit

-Measured value and uncertainty should be in same power of ten when given in scientific notation

-Absolute error/ uncertainty: size of error and units= x

-Relative/ Fractional Uncertainty: uncertainty/ measured value= x/ x

Keep 1-2 significant figures

-Precision is often reported by using relative/ fractional uncertainty, sometimes absolute value

-Relative error= (measured value- expected value)/ expected value

-Accuracy is often reported by using relative error

-Percentage uncertainty= relative uncertainty* 100%, keep 1-2 significant digits

-Percentage error/ discrepancy= relative error* 100%, keep 1-2 significant digits

**Error vs. Uncertainty**

-Error is the difference between the correct/accepted value, uncertainty is likely range of the true measurement

**Propagation of Error**

-Addition/ Subtraction: absolute uncertainty of the final result= sum of absolute uncertainties

-Formulas: (A A)+ (B B)= (A+B) (A + B)

(A A)- (B B)= (A-B) (A+ B)

-Multiplication/ Division: the percent uncertainty of final result= sum of percent uncertainties

-Formulas: (A A)* (B B)= (A*B) (A/A + B/B)* (A*B)

(A A)/ (B B)= (A/B) ( A/A+ B/B)* （A/B）

-For multiplication by an exact number, multiply the uncertainty by the exact same number

-x= Aya zb

x/ x= |a| (y/y) +|b| (z/z)

**Graphing Data**

-Independent variable: factor changed during the experiment, on x-axis

-Dependent variable: factor that depends on the independent variable, on y-axis

-Choose simple scales, like 1 square= 1N, 2N, 5N, or 10N

-Line of best fit: draw as close to all data points as possible

-Curve of best fit

-Anomalous point: outlier point; you can choose to ignore anomalous points

-Error bars: draw to scale, can be both horizontal and vertical

In this graph, blue: minimum slope line, yellow: maximum slope line, red: line of best fit

-Slope: rise/ run

## 1.5 Units, Standards, and the SI System

**The SI System**

-SI Base Quantities

Length: meter (m), mass: kilogram (kg), time: second (s), temperature: kelvin (K), amount of a substance: mole (mol), electric current: ampere (A), luminous intensity: candela (cd)

-SI derived units: units defined in terms of these seven base units

Speed: m/s, energy: Joule, electric charge: Coulomb, unified atomic mass

1J= 1kg* m2/s2; 1C= 1A* s, 1u= 1.6605* 10-27 kg

-Metric Prefixes

yotta, zetta, exa, peta, tera, giga, mega, kilo, hecto, deka, deci, centi, milli, micro, nano, pico, femto, atto, zepto, yocto

## 1.6 Converting Units

-Conversion factor: multiplier equal to 1

-Example: 1= 1kg/ 1000g

-to convert units, multiply the original measurement by a suitable conversion factor

## 1.7 Order of Magnitude

**Order of magnitude estimate**

-A rough estimate is made by rounding off all numbers to 1 significant figures and its power of 10. Do the calculation, and again keep 1 significant figure (still in power of 10)

-Your result can be accurate within a factor of 10 and often better

-Order of magnitude: the power of 10

# S1F-2 Chapter 4 Dynamics: Newton’s Laws of Motion

## Chapter 4 Dynamics: Newton’s Laws of Motion

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Final Physics H review guide (PA). Writers: Aryana Xu 9-1, Sharon Ren 9-3. Editor: Atticus Lee 9-6. Range: Chapter 1& Chapter 4. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**4-1 Force** **4-6** **Weight** **– The** **Force** **of** **Gravity** **and the Normal Force**

**Basic Idea of Force**

-Force: a push or pull exerted by one object on another (vector)

-Interaction between 2 objects

-System: to whom the force is exerted

-Agent: by whom the force is exerted

-Effects: cause a deformation (a change in dimension/shape) or to change the state of motion (change velocity)

-Unit: Newton (N) 1 N = 1 kg·m/s²

-Measurement device: spring scale

-Larger force → spring is stretched longer → larger reading

Three factors of forces:

- Magnitude: the strength of the force vector
- Direction: in which direction the force vector acts
- Point of application: the location the force is exerted

**Different Types of Forces**

Four fundamental forces:

- Strong Nuclear Force: The strongest force, responsible for holding protons and neutrons together in the nucleus of an atom
- Electromagnetic Force: This force acts between charged particles and is responsible for electricity, magnetism, and light
- Weak Nuclear Force: Responsible for processes like beta decay in nuclear reactions
- Gravity: The weakest force, it attracts objects with mass towards each other, governing the motion of planets and galaxies

-These forces govern how objects and particles interact in the universe

Contact forces and Field forces:

- Contact force: an object from the external world touches a system and thereby exerts a force on it
- Field force: exerted without contact

-Examples of Contact Forces: Friction, Drag force (air resistance / fluid resistance) Tension, Normal force, Spring force, Applied force

-Examples of Field Forces: Gravitational force, Electric force, Magnetic force

-Non-fundamental forces: Consequences of fundamental forces

Hooke’s Law: The magnitude of the force is directly proportional to the amount of stretch or compression within the limit of a spring

Formula: Fsp = –kx

Fsp — the force exerted by the spring on the attached object (N)

x — the displacement of the spring end from its equilibrium position (cm)

k — spring constant (N/cm)

“–” — F is opposite to x

Load (N) vs. Extension (cm)

-Extension is proportional to load from the origin to the elastic limit

Elastic limit: the point after which the spring will not return to its original shape

Types of Friction:

- Sliding Friction: the friction that occurs when two solid surfaces slide over each other

-Static Friction (Ffs): Caused by tendency of relative motion. (no relative motion between 2 objects in touch)

-Kinetic friction (Ffk): Caused by the relative motion (relative motion between 2 objects in touch)

- Rolling Friction: the friction that occurs when an object rolls over a surface (smaller than sliding friction)
- Fluid Friction: the friction that occurs when an object moves through a fluid

-Rolling < sliding; Fluid < sliding

Magnitude of Friction:

- Static Friction: the same as the force causing the relative motion.
- Maximum static friction (Ffs max = μs x FN)

-Ffs max — The max static friction

-μs — The coefficient of static friction (depends on how rough the surface is: μs ↑, rougher)

-FN — The normal force between two surfaces

**Equation for kinetic friction**

-Same objects: Ffk ≤ Ffs max

-Ffk = μk x FN

-coefficients of friction can also be bigger than 1, when the surface is sticky

Direction of friction: opposing the relative motion

Air resistance depends on:

- Shape of the object → Streamline: reduce friction
- Size of an object → Surface area ↑ → F_air ↑
- Speed of an object → Speed ↑ → F_air ↑
- Fluid type: viscosity → More viscous → F_air ↑

**Combining Forces**

-Draw vector sum graphically

- Method 1 (connect vectors from tip to tail)

-Place component vectors tip-to-tail

-Draw the resultant vector by connecting tail of first to tip of second

- Method 2 (Parallelogram rule)

-Place component vectors tail-to-tail

-Use the two vectors as adjacent sides and construct a parallelogram

-The diagonal from the common origin is the resultant vector

**Balanced forces**

-Equilibrant and balanced force → two forces are balanced

-Forces are equilibrant when two different forces act on the same object (same point of application), with the same magnitude, opposite direction, and acts on the same line

-Equilibrium: at rest / uniform motion (no acceleration)

## 4.2 Newton’s First Law of Motion

**Newton’s First Law**

-First Law:Every object continues in its state of rest, or of uniform velocity in a straight line, as long as no net force acts on it

-Inertia: Newton’s first law is also called the law of inertia

-Inertia is the tendency of an object to maintain its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line

-Not a force because forces are interactions between two objects

Inertia depends on: Mass, Larger mass → greater inertia

**Inertial Reference Frames (IRF)**

-In accelerating frame of reference, Newton’s First Law does not hold

-Reference frames in which Newton’s first law does hold are called: inertial reference frames (Law of inertia is valid in them)

-Earth’s frame of reference is close to IRF

-A reference frame moving with constant v relative to an IRF is also an IRF

-Reference frames where the law of inertia does not hold are called non-inertial reference frames

## 4.3 Mass

-Newton says: mass is a quantity of matter → Not well defined

-Inertial Mass: mass is equal to the ratio of the net force exerted on an object to its acceleration

-Mass: a measure of inertia of an object

-A measure of the object’s resistance to any type of force

-Gravitational mass: Mass as used in the law of universal gravitation determines the size of the gravitational force between two objects.

The principle of equivalence:

-Newton: inertial mass and gravitational mass are equal in magnitude.

-All experiments conducted so far have supported this principle.

## 4.4 Newton’s Second Law of Motion

-The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it, and is inversely proportional to its mass. The direction of the acceleration is in the direction of the net force acting on the object

Formula: ∑F = m x a

-∑ F — vector sum of all forces, net force (“Σ” = “sum of”)

Unit: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s²

-1 N: the force required to give a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s²

Steps to Utilize Newton’s Second Law:

- Identify the system
- Draw FBD, free body diagram (all the forces acting on the object)
- Find the net force, Fnet = F1 + F2 + F3…
- Use Newton’s Second Law, Fnet = m x a to find the acceleration.
- If necessary, use equations to find the velocity or position of the object

**Apparent weight**

-A spring scale measures weight, not mass

-The force exerted by the scale is called the apparent weight

Four elevator scenarios:

-Equilibrium → Fsp = Fg

-Accelerates upward → Fsp = m(g + a) → overweight

-Accelerates downward → Fsp = m(g – a) → lighter

-Free fall → Fsp = 0 → weightlessness

-Weightlessness ≠ zero gravity; means no contact force

## 4.5 Newton’s Third Law of Motion

-Interaction pair

–forces always come in pairs, FA on B =-FB on A

-opposite directions, equal magnitude, different systems and same type

-also called an action-reaction pair of forces

**Newton’s** **Third lLaw**

-Whenever one object exerts a force on a second object, the second exerts an equal force in the opposite direction on the first

-To every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction

Action-reaction examples:

- Paddle on water ↔ water on paddle
- Car tire pushes ground backward ↔ ground pushes car forward
- Water sprinkler reaction jets

Compare balanced force and action-reaction:

|  | Balanced-Force | Action-Reaction |
|---|---|---|
| Common | Same magnitude, opposite direction | Same magnitude, opposite direction |
| System | Same system (can cancel) | Different system (can’t cancel) |
| Timing | Not necessarily simultaneous | Always simultaneous |
| Force Type | Not necessarily same type | May cause acceleration |
| Effect on Motion | No acceleration | May cause acceleration |

## 4.7 Solving Problems with Newton’s Laws: Free-Body Diagrams

-Equilibrium Problems

-Definition: If net force = 0 → translational equilibrium

-Types: at rest or constant velocity

Conditions: ∑Fx = 0, ∑Fy = 0

**Connected Objects**

- Tension: if rope massless, tension same throughout
- System: group of objects studied together
- External forces: from outside system
- Internal forces: between objects in system (cancel in system analysis)

## 4.8 Problems Involving Friction, Inclines

-The maximum acceleration a vehicle can achieve without wheel slippage is limited by static friction:
${a}_{\text{max}}={\mu }_{s}g$.

-When a force is applied at an angle to a horizontal surface:

-Pushing downward increases the normal force: ${F}_{N}=mg+F\sin \theta$, which increases friction and makes motion harder

-Pulling upward decreases the normal force: ${F}_{N}=mg-F\sin \theta$, which reduces friction and makes motion easier

For an object at rest on an inclined plane:

-The coefficient of static friction required to prevent sliding is ${\mu }_{s}=\tan \theta$, where $\theta$is the incline angle

-This value is independent of mass

On an inclined plane with kinetic friction:

-Acceleration down the ramp is given by:

$$a=g(\sin \theta -{\mu }_{k}\cos \theta )$$

-Motion up or down the ramp depends on the direction and magnitude of applied forces, which must overcome both gravity and friction components

For connected objects on inclines (e.g., via a pulley):

-The system’s acceleration depends on the net gravitational component along the inclines minus the total kinetic friction

-Tension in the cord is found by analyzing one object at a time using Newton’s second law

For objects experiencing multiple non-aligned forces (e.g., parachutists):

-Resolve all forces into components

-Net force and acceleration are found using vector addition

In accelerating reference frames (e.g., a car with a pendulum):

-The pendulum angle relates to acceleration by $\theta ={\tan }^{-1}(a/g)$

-At constant velocity (zero acceleration), the pendulum hangs vertically ($\theta ={0}^{∘}$).

# S2M-1 Semester 2 Midterm review: Chapter 5 & Chapter 6

## Semester 2 Midterm review: Chapter 5 & Chapter 6

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 2 Midterm Physics H review guide (PA). Writers: Aryana Xu 9-1, Lorenzo Huang 9-3. Editor: Kenny Yuan 9-6. Range: Chapter 5 & Chapter 6. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## Chapter 5: Circular Motion; Gravitation

## 5.1 Kinematics of Uniform Circular Motion

**Uniform Circular Motion**

-Uniform circular motion: an object that moves in a circle at constant speed is said to experience uniform circular motion

-Velocity vector: always tangent to the path

-Centripetal acceleration (aR): also known as radial acceleration, always points to the center of the circle

-Formula: aR= v2/r= 4π2r/ T2=4π2f2r

-On a rigid body experiencing UCM, two points on the body has the same frequency and period

## 5.2 Dynamics of Uniform Circular Motion

**Centripetal Force**

-Centripetal force (FR or FC): the net force toward the center of the circle during circular motion

-Centripetal force is not a new force, it is the net force of circular motion

-Can be made up of normal force, gravity, tension, etc.

-Formula: Fnet= FR= maR= m v2/r= mω2r= m 4π2r/ T2

**Centrifugal Force**

-Centrifugal force: not an actual force

-the feeling of being pushed away from the center is due to inertia

## 5.3 Highway Curves, Banked and Unbanked

**Unbanked Curve**

-Formula: Fnet= Ffs= FR

-The centripetal force is provided by static friction

-There is never a centrifugal force

-If the friction force is not sufficient, the car will tend to move more nearly in a straight line according to Newton’s 1st law (inertia)

-As long as the tires do not slip, the friction is static

-If the tires start to slip, the friction is kinetic

Consequences:

- The Ffk< Ffs, so the car can’t turn as sharply
- The Ffs points toward the circle center, but the Ffk opposes the direction of motion, making it difficult to regain control of the car and continue around the curve

-Formula for unbanked curve: vmax= √(μsgr)

-Maximum speed is independent of mass

**Banked Curve**

-Banked turns: using a slope/ hill/ angle to help us turn safely

-Banked curves helps keep cards from skidding

-For every banked curve: there is one speed v where no friction is required

-Formula for designed speed in banked curve: v= √(gr tanθ)

-Designed speed is independent of mass

-If v> designed speed: Ffs appears to increase the Fnetx

If v< designed speed: Ffs appears to decrease th Fnetx

-Function of banked turns:

1. To allow us to not rely on friction for turning on a road

2. To allow planes to turn, as they do not have friction

3. To allow race cars to go at faster speeds

4. To help with the wear and tear of your tires

## 5.6 Newton’s Law of Universal Gravitation

**Newton’s Law of Universal Gravitation**

-Statement: Every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force that is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. This force acts along the line joining the two particles.

-Formula: ${F}_{G}=G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{{r}^{2}}$

-G: universal gravitational constant, G=6.67 x 10-11 N·m2 / kg2

-In 1798, Englishman Henry Cavendish measured the gravitational force between two objects, found universal gravitational constant

-The device was invented by John Michell

-Conditions to apply to calculation

1. Two particles (objects with no size and no shape) separated distance r away

2. Extended objects: small size compared to the distance r

3. Extended objects: when r and the sizes are comparable, integral calculus is needed

-Newton was able to show that the gravitational force exerted on a particle outside a uniform sphere is the same as if the entire mass of the sphere was concentrated at its center.

## 5.7 Gravity Near the Earth Surface

**Acceleration due to gravity on Earth’s surface**

-g=9.8m/s2

-mE=5.98*10^24 kg

**Acceleration due to gravity on other planet**

-Formula: g= GM/ r2

**Acceleration due to gravity far away from Earth’s surface**

-Formula: a=g (rE/r)2

-When moving an object farther from Earth’s center, r becomes larger, the acceleration due to gravity is reduced

## 5.8 Satellites and “Weightlessness”

**Newton’s thought** **experiment**

-Ignore air resistance

-Projectile launched horizontally

-If the horizontal speed v is high enough, curve of its path matches the surface of the Earth. The cannonball would be able to orbit the Earth

**Speed and period for a satellite**

-Satellites are put into orbit at very high speeds, this way, as it falls towards earth, it is also moving horizontally, causing it to not crash into Earth.

-A satellite in an orbit that is always the same height above earth moves in uniform circular motion

-Gravitational force provides the centripetal force

-Formulas: speed- v= √(G mcentral/ r)

Period- T= 2π√(r3/ G mcentral)

-The “weightlessness” experienced by people in a satellite orbit close to earth is the same apparent weightlessness experienced in a free fall elevator. Weight is still present, but the apparent weight, or normal force is 0. Astronauts experience weightlessness as the shuttle and everything in it falls freely towards Earth together.

**Gravitational field**

-Any object with mass is surrounded by a gravitational field in which another object experiences a force due to the interaction between its mass and the gravitational field g at its location.

-Calculations for gravitational field forces is the same as calculations for the gravitational acceleration

-Formula: gravitational field g= GM/ r2

Unit: N/kg or m/s2

## 5.9 Kepler’s Law and Newton’s Synthesis

-Time: more than a half century before Newton proposed his 3 laws of motion and his law of universal gravitation

-German astronomer Johannes Kepler

-Kepler’s first law: The path of each planet about the sun is an ellipse with the sun at one focus

-Kepler’s second law: An imaginary line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas during equal intervals of time

Each planet moves faster when it is closer to the Sun and slower when it is farther away from the Sun

-Kepler’s third law: the square of the ratio of the periods is equal to the cube of the ratio of their average distance

-Formulas: (TA/ TB)2= (rA/rB)3

T= 2π√(r3/GmS)

**6: Work and Energy**

**6-1 & 6-2Work done by a varying/constant force**

Work: the product of the force component parallel to the displacement and the magnitude of the displacement

-Scalar(no direction), but can be pos/neg

Symbol: W

Unit: Joule (J)

Formula for work:

W= Fdcosθ

In this formula, θ is the angle between the direction of the force and the displacement

-When a force is perpendicular to the displacement, no work is done by that force.

Work done by a varying force:

Found by the graphical method - draw an F-d graph

-The area between the line and the d axis is the work done by that force

Area above d axis: positive

Area below d axis: negative

**6-3: Kinetic Energy and Work-Energy Principle**

Energy: The ability of an object to produce a change in itself or the world around

Translational kinetic energy represents the energy due to movement through space, while

kinetic energy implies both translational kinetic energy and rotational kinetic energy.

Translational Kinetic energy:

-The energy of motion

Symbol: KE

Unit: J(Joule)

Work energy principle:

- When all work done on the system is converted into kinetic energy: W=ΔKE

-The net work done on an object is equal to the object’s kinetic energy

-Only valid if W is the net work done

**6-4: Potential Energy**

Potential energy: The energy associated with forces that depend on the position or

configuration of an object relative to the surroundings

Please note that PA materials are student-created and for reference only.

1. Gravitational potential energy

- The stored energy in a system resulting from the gravitational force on the object

Symbol: GPE

Formula: GPE=mgh

m: mass

g: gravitational acceleration

h: height above reference level

2. Elastic potential energy

-The stored energy in an object as a result of its change in shape

-Can be stored in springs, rubber bands, etc...

Hooke’s Law:

The spring force is directly proportional to the displacement if the spring and opposite to the

direction of the displacement of the spring

Formula: FS=-kx

k: spring constant, unit: N/m

x: displacement (compressed or stretched distance)

Spring force is a restoring force: the force is in the direction opposite to the displacement,

restoring the spring to its natural length

Formula for elastic potential energy:

EPE=(k(x)2)/2

-A point with zero PEe (the spring’s natural position), should be chosen as reference point
